pericopes.text: Now I, Moroni, after having made an end of abridging the account of the people of Jared, I had supposed not to have written more, but I have not as yet perished; and I make not myself known to the Lamanites, lest they should destroy me.

links.text: Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me. And there stood no man with him, while Joseph made himself known unto his brethren.

provenance.other: The King James Bible makes a person the reflexive object of 'make known' in very few places. “made himself known” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 45:1; “make myself known” occurs in exactly two, Numbers 12:6 and Ezekiel 35:11, and both are God disclosing himself, not a man concealing himself. “known unto his brethren” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 45:1, and “known to his brethren” in exactly one, Acts 7:13, which is Stephen retelling the same scene. Within the Book of Mormon the reflexive form is unique to this verse; the other eleven occurrences of 'make known' are all transitive and all have a message, not a self, for their object.
provenance.alternative: Acts 7:13, 'And at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren', is the same episode in the New Testament and is the reason mediation-check.py was run here. Its verdict should be disregarded and the reason is worth recording: the tool reports one decisive point for Acts, namely that the Book of Mormon lacks Genesis's word 'himself'. It lacks it because it has 'myself'. The reflexive is present and it is the whole point of the contact; Acts has the passive, 'was made known', with no reflexive at all. This is the pronoun trap ADJUDICATING §4 names — the checker ignores short common words and so cannot see that one reflexive has been swapped for another. Read by hand the divergence goes the other way, and the mediation is direct-OT. The larger alternative is that there is no borrowing here at all: see whyNot.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis, and of the inverting kind. Recover Genesis 45 and the sentence is the hinge of the Joseph story: the brother whom his brethren had sold, hidden from them under another name in the land that fed them, at last stops hiding — 'I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt' — and the disclosure turns out to be their deliverance, 'for God did send me before you to preserve life' (45:4-5). Moroni's clause runs the same machinery backwards. He is the last of his house, hidden among the people who destroyed it, and what he says is that he will *not* make himself known: the recognition scene is refused, because in his case being recognised is being killed. What survives of Joseph's ending is displaced into the record itself. Three verses later the concealed brother says why he writes at all — 'that perhaps they may be of worth unto my brethren, the Lamanites, in some future day' — which is Joseph's line about preserving life, addressed to the same relation, deferred by centuries and entrusted to a book instead of a face. The Book of Mormon has spent 2 Nephi 3 on Lehi's descent from Joseph and on a Joseph who is a prophet of the latter days; the last writer in the book closes it by taking Joseph's one gesture and declining to perform it.

links.note: 'I make not myself known to the Lamanites, lest they should destroy me.' The English idiom is ordinary enough that a reader may pass over it, which is why the counts matter: making *oneself* known is a rare construction in the King James Bible, and its one narrative instance is Joseph before his brethren at Genesis 45:1. Moroni's sentence has the same three elements — a man, the reflexive disclosure, and the estranged kindred who are its object — with the verb negated, and it supplies the kinship term itself at 1:4, where the Lamanites are 'my brethren'. Nothing else of Genesis 45 is reproduced, so this is catalogued as an allusion and not higher: the case is one distinctive construction plus a situation that answers the source at every point by reversing it. Recorded because the reversal is the argument. A reader who hears the Joseph scene behind Moroni's refusal is hearing something the catalogue can at least locate, and a reader who does not is told here where it was located and how thin the thread is.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is a negated reflexive verb and nothing else. 'Make oneself known' is unmarked modern English as well as King James English, and a writer describing a fugitive who conceals his identity from his enemies could reach the phrase with no scripture in view at all; the KJV counts establish that the construction is rare in the KJV, not that it is rare in English. The kinship term that carries most of the weight is three verses away and is the Book of Mormon's standing designation for the Lamanites, used hundreds of times, so it cannot be claimed as a borrowed element. Withdraw this row if a reader is unwilling to let situation do that much of the work.

pericopes.text: For behold, their wars are exceeding fierce among themselves; and because of their hatred, they put to death every Nephite that will not deny the Christ.
And I, Moroni, will not deny the Christ; wherefore, I wander whithersoever I can, for the safety of mine own life.

links.text: Then David and his men, which were about six hundred, arose and departed out of Keilah, and went whithersoever they could go. And it was told Saul that David was escaped from Keilah; and he forbare to go forth.

provenance.other: “whithersoever” occurs in 29 KJV verses, and in twenty-eight of them the movement is commanded, sent or accompanied — 'whithersoever thou goest', 'whithersoever thou sendest us', 'the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went'. The adverb is bound to a second person or to providence. “whithersoever they could” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 23:13, and it is the only place the KJV attaches the word to the fugitive's own bare ability rather than to anyone's direction. Moroni's 'whithersoever I can' is that construction with the person changed. “whithersoever I can” occurs in no KJV verse, and 'for the safety of' occurs in none either; “mine own life” occurs in exactly one, 2 Samuel 18:13, in an unrelated setting.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is the pursuit. 1 Samuel 23:13 is the verse at which David stops being a commander and becomes a fugitive: he has just saved Keilah and learned that Keilah will hand him over, so he leaves with his men and goes nowhere in particular, and the next two verses say what that life consists of — 'Saul sought him every day, but God delivered him not into his hand', and 'David saw that Saul was come out to seek his life'. Recover that and Moroni's half-sentence acquires its second clause. He wanders whithersoever he can because someone is looking for him every day, and the reason he gives — 'for the safety of mine own life' — is 1 Samuel 23:15's 'to seek his life' answered from the other side. The suppressed correspondence is the one Moroni cannot say and 1 Samuel does: that the man hunted in this way was not delivered into the hand of the man hunting him. Moroni has already said as much in his own words at 1:1, 'I have not as yet perished', and the 'as yet' is where the two texts differ. David's preservation ends in a throne; Moroni's is a stay of execution he does not expect to outlast.

links.note: 'I wander whithersoever I can, for the safety of mine own life.' The King James Bible uses 'whithersoever' twenty-nine times and almost always of directed movement; exactly once it uses it of a hunted man's undirected flight, at 1 Samuel 23:13, where David and his men 'went whithersoever they could go'. Moroni's clause is that idiom in the first person singular — the same adverb, the same modal of bare ability, the same absence of any destination — and it is doing the same narrative work, marking the point at which a leader with no people left becomes a man simply staying alive. The situations agree without being made to: a solitary survivor, an enemy who has taken the country, movement with no object but not being found. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion, since what is reproduced is a construction rather than a clause; the strength of the row is that the construction is a KJV singleton and that the singleton is about precisely this.

links.text: But he spake the more vehemently, If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise. Likewise also said they all.

provenance.other: “I will not deny” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 14:31. “deny thee” occurs in exactly three — Proverbs 30:9, Matthew 26:35 and Mark 14:31 — and only the last two are about denying Christ. The rarity is not an artifact of a rare word: 'deny' is common enough in the KJV, and its usual home is exactly this subject, so the count is a fact about how the KJV phrases a vow of loyalty rather than about vocabulary.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 26:35 is the same vow in the same scene — 'Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee' — and mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence between the two, because the synoptic parallels do not differ at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces. The choice is therefore made on word order alone and is worth only what that is worth: Moroni has 'will not deny' with the subject in front of it, which is Mark's order, while Matthew's 'yet will I not deny' inverts subject and auxiliary after the concessive. Either evangelist gives the same reading of the verse, and a reader who prefers Matthew loses nothing but the singleton.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis, and the recovered context is unflattering to no one but is very sharp. Mark 14:31 is Peter's boast in Gethsemane, spoken 'the more vehemently' and endorsed by all the disciples, and the whole point of the verse in Mark is that it is about to be false: within thirty verses Peter has denied him thrice and gone out and wept. The KJV's one instance of a man saying he will not deny Christ is therefore a promise that fails, and it is uttered by someone in no immediate danger. Moroni's use of the same words puts the sentence back in the mouth of a man for whom the condition Peter only imagined — 'if I should die with thee' — is the actual terms of the offer, since 1:2 has just said that the Lamanites 'put to death every Nephite that will not deny the Christ'. The suppressed correspondence is a correction: Peter says it at the last supper and breaks it by morning; Moroni says it as a man already under sentence, and the following clause is not a denial but a flight.

links.note: 'And I, Moroni, will not deny the Christ.' “I will not deny” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 14:31, where Peter swears he will not deny Jesus though he die with him — which is the same proposition, under the same condition of death, that Moroni states in the previous verse as the standing Lamanite policy and here accepts for himself. The object differs: Peter says 'thee' to Christ's face, Moroni writes 'the Christ', which is the Book of Mormon's own title and not the KJV's phrase (see the exclusion at 1:2). So what is borrowed is the vow and not the sentence. Catalogued at moderate rather than high because the four shared words are common ones in a common order and the count, though real, could be coincidence in a way that 1 Samuel 23:13's 'whithersoever they could' could not; and because the object, which is the part that would have settled it, is the part the Book of Mormon supplies itself.
links.whyNot: The whole verbal case is four ordinary words. A writer with no verse in view who wanted to say that a man refused to deny Christ would very likely produce 'will not deny' unaided, and the KJV's single occurrence reflects how rarely the KJV has occasion to put the vow in the first person, not how distinctive the wording is. The doctrinal background — Matthew 10:33, 2 Timothy 2:12 — is available to the Book of Mormon without Mark, and the phrase 'deny the Christ' is already the Book of Mormon's own formula at Alma 30:39, 3 Nephi 29:5 and Mormon 9:3, so this verse may be nothing more than its author's fourth use of a phrase he had used three times before.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, I write a few more things, contrary to that which I had supposed: for I had supposed not to have written any more; but I write a few more things, that perhaps they may be of worth unto my brethren, the Lamanites, in some future day, according to the will of the Lord.
The words of Christ, which he spake unto his disciples, the twelve whom he had chosen, as he laid his hands upon them.

links.text: And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them; and they spake with tongues, and prophesied.

provenance.route: Acts 19:6 (with Acts 8:17) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “laid his hands upon them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 19:6, where Paul's hand-laying is immediately followed by the coming of the Holy Ghost. The nearest competitor, Mark 10:16, reads ‘put his hands upon them’ and blesses children. The plural form “laid their hands on” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which Acts 8:17 and Acts 6:6 are the ordinations.
provenance.significance: The scene this verse summarises is 3 Nephi 18:36, and there Christ ‘touched with his hand the disciples whom he had chosen, one by one’. Moroni is not copying that sentence; he is retelling it in the King James Bible's technical vocabulary for the same act. Touching becomes laying on of hands — which is to say that between 3 Nephi and Moroni the gesture has become an ordinance, and the words it acquires on the way are Luke's words for what Paul did at Ephesus.

links.note: ‘As he laid his hands upon them.’ Moroni's heading for the ordinance uses the KJV's one exact form of the phrase, and uses it where the earlier Book of Mormon account of the same moment (3 Nephi 18:36) had said ‘touched with his hand … one by one’. Acts 19:6 is the KJV verse where that gesture and the reception of the Holy Ghost stand in one sentence, which is the whole content of this chapter; Acts 8:17 supplies the plural form that Moroni 2:3 and Moroni 3:2 then use for the disciples doing it in turn. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six extended quotations.

links.text: Until the day in which he was taken up, after that he through the Holy Ghost had given commandments unto the apostles whom he had chosen:

provenance.route: Acts 1:2 → KJV → 3 Nephi 18:36 → Moroni 2:1, or Acts 1:2 → KJV → Moroni 2:1 directly; the two cannot be separated on the wording
provenance.other: “whom he had chosen” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 105:26 (Moses and Aaron) and Acts 1:2. Only Acts 1:2 has the twelve, and only Acts 1:2 joins them to the Holy Ghost and to commandments given after the resurrection. Note the enum limitation: the mediation vocabulary has `OT-via-earlier-BoM` but no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage, which is the shape of this case, so it is recorded as `uncertain` and the route is written out.
provenance.significance: Acts 1:2 is Luke's one-sentence summary of exactly the situation Moroni is heading: a risen Christ, before departing, giving commandments through the Holy Ghost to the apostles whom he had chosen. Moroni 2 is that sentence unpacked into an ordinance.

links.note: ‘The twelve whom he had chosen.’ The phrase is already at 3 Nephi 18:36 (‘the disciples whom he had chosen’), so this verse's proximate model may be the earlier Book of Mormon passage rather than the Bible — which is why the confidence is moderate and the mediation is left open. What makes it worth recording anyway is that the KJV has the phrase twice and one of the two, Acts 1:2, is the verse where the chosen ones are apostles, the giving is post-resurrection, and the Holy Ghost is the medium. Every element of Moroni 2:1 is in it. Luke 6:13 supplies the numeral: ‘of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles’, and Moroni 2:2 ends ‘for thus do mine apostles’.

pericopes.text: And he called them by name, saying, Ye shall call on the Father in my name, in mighty prayer; and after that ye have done this, ye shall have power that on him whom ye shall lay your hands, ye shall give the Holy Ghost; and in my name shall ye give it: for thus do mine apostles.

links.text: Saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost.

provenance.route: Acts 8:17-19 → KJV → Book of Mormon. The catalogue already reads 3 Nephi 18:37 on the same passage; Moroni 2:2 is verbally closer to Acts 8:19 than 3 Nephi 18:37 is, so it reaches the Bible on its own account rather than through the earlier Book of Mormon verse.
provenance.other: “this power that on” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:19, and “he may receive the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “the Holy Ghost was given” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:18, which also supplies ‘the apostles' hands’ for this verse's closing ‘for thus do mine apostles’. Acts 8:14-19 is the King James Bible's only passage that speaks of a power to confer the Holy Ghost by touch as something transferable.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis of the uncomfortable kind. Recover the context of the one KJV verse that frames the power this way and the speaker is Simon Magus, and the next verse is ‘Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money’. Moroni 2:2 takes Simon's sentence, inverts its direction — the disciples do not receive the Spirit by hands laid on them, they give it by hands they lay — and puts it in Christ's mouth as a grant, conditioned on prayer in the Father's name rather than on money. The words a sorcerer used to ask for the power are the words in which it is lawfully given.

links.note: ‘Ye shall have power that on him whom ye shall lay your hands, ye shall give the Holy Ghost.’ Set beside Acts 8:19, ‘Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost’: the same four-part frame in the same order — power, the ‘that on…’ relative, the laying of hands, the Holy Ghost — with the recipient and the agent exchanged. It is not a reproduced clause and is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, but the frame is a KJV singleton and the substitutions are systematic rather than incidental. 3 Nephi 18:37 promised these words and withheld them (‘the multitude heard not the words which he spake… I will shew unto you hereafter that this record is true’); Moroni 2 is the promised delivery, and what arrives is Acts 8. Note the 1830 reading ‘that on him whom ye shall lay your hands’, where 1920 deletes ‘that’ and reads ‘on whom ye shall lay your hands’: the first edition keeps the ‘power … that on’ construction that is Acts 8:19's alone, and the later edition erases it.

links.text: And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

provenance.route: John 16:23 fused with 1 Peter 1:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the Father in my name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 15:16 and John 16:23, both of them promises made to the twelve in the upper room. “call on the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 1:17. tools/mediation-check.py run on the three returns divergences pointing both ways — the Book of Mormon has 1 Peter's verb (‘call on’, not ‘ask’) and John's object and outcome (‘the Father in my name … give it’) — which is the tool's signature for a composite rather than a choice between candidates.
provenance.significance: John 16:23 is the promise; Moroni 2:2 is its discharge. What is asked for in John is unspecified (‘whatsoever ye shall ask’) and what is given is unspecified (‘he will give it you’); here the pronoun acquires a referent — the thing asked for and given is the Holy Ghost — and the promise made to the twelve at the supper is executed by twelve other men on another continent.

links.note: ‘Ye shall call on the Father in my name, in mighty prayer; … and in my name shall ye give it.’ Two KJV verses hold ‘the Father in my name’ and John 16:23 is the one that continues ‘he will give it you’ — so John supplies not only the prayer formula but the bare ‘give it’ that Moroni's clause repeats with the agency reversed: in John the Father gives it, here the disciples do, in the same name. The verb is not John's, though. ‘Ask’ has become ‘call on’, which in the KJV is joined to ‘the Father’ only at 1 Peter 1:17, and the two are fused into one clause. Compare 3 Nephi 18:19-20, which had already put John 16:23 into Christ's mouth in the Book of Mormon (‘whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is right … it shall be given unto you’); the phrasing there is John's alone, and the 1 Peter verb enters only here.

pericopes.text: Now Christ spake these words unto them at the time of his first appearing; and the multitude heard it not, but the disciples heard it; and on as many as they laid their hands, fell the Holy Ghost.

links.text: Then laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost.

provenance.route: Acts 8:16-17, with the verb of Acts 10:44 / 11:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “laid their hands on” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Mark 14:46, Acts 5:18, Acts 6:6, Acts 13:3); “the Holy Ghost fell” occurs in exactly two, Acts 10:44 and Acts 11:15; “fallen upon none” occurs in exactly one, Acts 8:16. Acts 8:16-17 is the only KJV place where the falling and the hand-laying belong to one narrative — ‘as yet he was fallen upon none of them … then laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost’ — which is exactly the pair Moroni's clause holds. Acts 10:44 also shares ‘spake these words’ and the hearing: “spake these words” occurs in exactly four KJV verses.
provenance.significance: Acts 8 and Acts 10 are the New Testament's two test cases for how the Spirit arrives, and they disagree: at Samaria it will not come until apostolic hands are laid on, at Caesarea it falls on the hearers with no hands at all and settles the question of the Gentiles. Moroni 2:3 writes the sentence in Acts 10's grammar — the Spirit is the subject and it falls — and gives it Acts 8's condition, hands. The verse resolves in one clause a tension the KJV leaves standing across two chapters.

links.note: ‘And on as many as they laid their hands, fell the Holy Ghost.’ The inverted order, with the Holy Ghost after its verb, is the tell: the KJV writes ‘the Holy Ghost fell on’ twice, both in the Cornelius material, and writes the hand-laying that produces the Spirit at Acts 8:17. This clause has both, and it is the only new material in the verse — the rest of Moroni 2:3 restates 3 Nephi 18:36-37 almost phrase for phrase (‘the multitude heard not the words which he spake’ becomes ‘the multitude heard it not, but the disciples heard it’), so the Book of Mormon's own account supplies the frame and Acts supplies the sentence Moroni adds to it. The report-form and the reversed word order together make this a report of the ordinance working, on the model of the KJV's own reports.

pericopes.text: The manner which the disciples, which were called the Elders of the church, ordained priests and teachers.

links.text: And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church.

provenance.other: 'The elders of the church' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 20:17 and James 5:14, and in neither Testament anywhere else; the longer run 'called the elders of the church' is a KJV singleton at Acts 20:17. Inside the Book of Mormon the phrase occurs twice, at Alma 4:16 and here.
provenance.significance: Moroni is writing the church-order appendix his father's book lacks, and the office he has to name first is one the Nephite record has barely used. He names it by borrowing the one clause in the King James Bible where a church's elders are summoned and addressed as such — Paul at Miletus, whose speech to those elders (Acts 20:28) is the New Testament's charge to men set over a flock. Recover that context and Moroni 3 acquires an apostolic farewell behind it, which is precisely the situation of the man writing: the last officer of a destroyed church setting down how its officers were made.

links.note: The 1830 reads 'the disciples, which were called the Elders of the church' — a relative clause whose four operative words reproduce the KJV singleton at Acts 20:17 in order. The verb is doing different work in each place (Paul 'called' the elders to him; Moroni's disciples 'were called' by that title), and that shift is the reason this is catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation: the run is verbatim but the syntax has been repurposed. It sits well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not among his thirty-six. James 5:14 supplies the same four words and is not the source — see the register at this verse.

pericopes.text: After they had prayed unto the Father in the name of Christ, they laid their hands upon them, and said,

links.text: Whom they set before the apostles: and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.

provenance.other: 'They laid their hands' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: 2 Chronicles 29:23, Mark 14:46 and Acts 6:6. Only Acts 6:6 is an ordination, and only Acts 6:6 puts prayer first. Acts 13:3 and 14:23 have the same order of operations in different words ('when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them'; 'when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed').
provenance.significance: Acts 6 is the New Testament's one narrated ordination to a subordinate office — the seven set over the tables so that the apostles may keep to prayer and the word. Moroni 3 is the Nephite church's rite for its two subordinate offices. The suppressed correspondence is that in Acts the men ordained this way are not the leaders; the rite is what the church does when authority has to be delegated downward, which is exactly the setting Moroni is describing and exactly the situation he is in.

links.note: The candidate list ranks 2 Chronicles 29:23 far above this verse, because 'laid their hands upon them' is a KJV singleton there and Acts reads 'on them' rather than 'upon them'. The ranking is wrong and the reason is sequence. mediation-check.py against Numbers 8:10 returns one decisive point and it is this one: Moroni's clause is 'After they had prayed … they laid their hands upon them', and 'when they had prayed, they laid their hands' is Acts 6:6's whole second half, word for word except the preposition. No other verse in the Bible subordinates prayer to the laying on of hands in that order. The preposition is worth flagging rather than explaining away: 'upon them' is the form of the sin-offering verse the machine preferred, so the clause may be carrying a word from the Levitical rite inside a sentence built on the apostolic one. On the internal route, Moroni 2:2 has the risen Christ authorise the same gesture two chapters earlier, so this ordinance is not being derived from Acts in the narrative's own terms; the wording still is.

pericopes.text: In the name of Jesus Christ I ordain you to be a priest; (or if he be a teacher,) I ordain you to be a teacher, to preach repentance and remission of sins through Jesus Christ, by the endurance of faith on his name to the end. Amen.

links.text: And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.

provenance.other: 'Repentance and remission of sins' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:47. The bare 'remission of sins' occurs in seven verses (Matthew 26:28, Mark 1:4, Luke 3:3, Luke 24:47, Acts 2:38, Acts 10:43, Romans 3:25), so it is the conjunction with 'repentance', not the phrase itself, that identifies the source.
provenance.significance: Luke 24:47 is the risen Christ's commission, and what it commissions is preaching — 'should be preached in his name'. Moroni's ordination formula ordains a man 'to preach repentance and remission of sins through Jesus Christ'. The office is being defined by the content of the Emmaus-evening charge, so that a Nephite priest is made by being given the last instruction Luke's Jesus gives before the ascension. That the charge is 'among all nations' is the unstated half, and it is the half a book addressed to a future gentile readership would want.

links.note: Five words in order from the one KJV verse that has them, inside a sentence whose subject is preaching, which is Luke 24:47's subject. Acts 2:38 shares 'remission of sins' and 'the name of Jesus Christ' with this verse and scores on both, but it is a baptismal formula, not a commission to preach, and the distinctive run belongs to Luke; the register records the displacement. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his thirty-six. The rest of the verse — 'by the endurance of faith on his name to the end' — is Moroni's own idiom, recurring at Moroni 8:3 and nowhere in the KJV.

pericopes.text: And after this manner did they ordain priests and teachers, according to the gifts and callings of God unto men; and they ordained them by the power of the Holy Ghost, which was in them.

links.text: For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.

provenance.other: 'The gifts and calling of God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:29; 'gifts and calling' occurs nowhere else in the King James Bible, and the plural 'callings' occurs in the KJV not at all. 'Gifts and callings' occurs once in the Book of Mormon, here.
provenance.significance: Romans 11:29 is the clause with which Paul refuses to let God's election of Israel be revoked — the gifts and calling are 'without repentance', that is, God does not change his mind about them. Moroni ordains 'according to the gifts and callings of God unto men', and if the Pauline context is recovered, the ordinance he is recording acquires the irrevocability of the verse it borrows: the offices of a church about to be annihilated are conferred under the one formula in scripture that says a divine calling is not withdrawn. Nothing in Moroni 3 says this. The four borrowed words do.

links.note: Not in the dossier's top twenty-four — the n-gram stream missed it, as CONVENTIONS §9 predicts it will when the shared run is short and the Book of Mormon has altered a word. The alteration is the pluralisation: Paul's singular 'calling' becomes 'callings', which is why no contiguous four-word window matched, and it is also the strongest evidence for dependence rather than coincidence, since 'callings' is not a King James word at all. 'Unto men' is Moroni's addition and turns Paul's abstract noun-phrase into a distribution of offices.

links.text: Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.

provenance.route: 1 Timothy 4:14 (with 2 Timothy 1:6) → KJV → Book of Mormon, if at all
provenance.other: Neither pastoral verse shares a distinctive string with Moroni 3. The contact is that 1 Timothy 4:14 holds all three elements of this chapter's rite in one sentence — a gift, a body of elders (presbytery), and the laying on of hands — and that 2 Timothy 1:6 states the same rite as a gift 'which is in thee by the putting on of my hands', against Moroni 3:4's 'by the power of the Holy Ghost, which was in them'.
provenance.significance: If the correspondence is real, the whole of Moroni 3 is one New Testament sentence unfolded into an ordinance: 3:1 supplies the presbytery, 3:2 the laying on of hands, 3:4 the gift that is in them. That is the shape of a rubric derived from a text rather than described from practice.

links.note: Recorded because the pastoral epistles are where a reader will look for this chapter's background and the catalogue should say what it found there. Across three verses Moroni 3 assembles the elements 1 Timothy 4:14 holds in one, and the relative clause of Moroni 3:4 ('which was in them') stands where 2 Timothy 1:6 has 'which is in thee'. It is a structural correspondence and it is offered as no more than that.
links.whyNot: There is no distinctive shared wording anywhere. 'Which was in them' is a KJV singleton only at 1 Peter 1:11, where it is connective tissue and not a source; 'gift' is universal; the KJV's 'presbytery' and 'putting on' appear nowhere in the Book of Mormon. The ordinance's shape is also supplied internally: Moroni 2:2 has the risen Christ authorise the laying on of hands to give the Holy Ghost two chapters earlier, so the sequence prayer-hands-gift needs no Pauline source to explain it. Withdraw this row if the verbal case at 3:1, 3:2 and 3:4 is judged sufficient on its own, which it may well be.

pericopes.text: The manner of their elders and priests administering the flesh and blood of Christ unto the church. And they administered it according to the commandments of Christ; wherefore we know that the manner to be true: and the elder priest did minister it.

links.text: Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 11:27, with 1 Corinthians 10:16 and John 6:54-56 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “body and blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 11:27, and “guilty of the body” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “blood of Christ” occurs in exactly four KJV verses and only 1 Corinthians 10:16 is eucharistic; that verse also holds “the bread which we break”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 6:54 and 6:56. Against all of that, “flesh and blood” as a fixed pair occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Matthew 16:17, 1 Corinthians 15:50, Galatians 1:16, Ephesians 6:12, Hebrews 2:14 — and in every one of them it means human nature, never sacramental food.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 10:16 alone, if the genitive ‘of Christ’ is weighted above the coordinate pair.
provenance.significance: Moroni's chapter heading names the thing administered as ‘the flesh and blood of Christ’, and the KJV cannot supply that phrase: it has the pair only as ‘the body and blood of the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 11:27) and it has ‘flesh’ for the eucharistic object only in John 6, where the two nouns are never coordinated but always governed by separate verbs — eateth my flesh, drinketh my blood. Moroni's phrase is the Pauline pair with the Johannine noun. That is exactly the weld already catalogued at 3 Nephi 18:29, where Paul's warning about eating ‘unworthily’ is fitted to John's ‘whoso eateth’ and John's flesh; here the same fusion has hardened into a rubric, the name a scribe uses for the ordinance itself rather than a sentence a speaker composes. The interesting consequence is invisible in the KJV: because ‘flesh and blood’ everywhere else in the New Testament means what a mortal is made of, Moroni's title for the sacrament reads, against its own intention, as the administering of Christ's humanity to the church.

links.note: The verse is a rubric, not narration, and its verbal contact with any one KJV verse is short. What carries the link is that the object of the ordinance is named as a coordinate pair of Christ's own substance, a construction the KJV performs once, at 1 Corinthians 11:27, with ‘body’ where Moroni has ‘flesh’ and ‘the Lord’ where Moroni has ‘Christ’. Both substitutions are traceable: ‘of Christ’ is 1 Corinthians 10:16's form, and ‘flesh’ is John 6's. The rest of the verse — ‘administered it according to the commandments of Christ; wherefore we know the manner to be true’ — has no KJV source and is Moroni's own editorial voice. Catalogued at moderate because the argument is about a construction rather than a run of words; a reader who wants a verbal link here will not find one.
links.whyNot: No shared run longer than three words with any of the three proposed sources. The strongest machine candidates for this verse (Deuteronomy 17:4 and 22:20, ‘be true and the’) are dating-clause boilerplate and are filed in the register. If ‘flesh and blood of Christ’ is simply Nephite idiom — the Book of Mormon uses ‘flesh and blood’ of Christ's body elsewhere without visible Pauline pressure — then nothing here is borrowed and the row should be withdrawn.

pericopes.text: And they did kneel down with the church, and pray to the Father in the name of Christ, saying,

links.text: Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ;

provenance.other: “the Father in the name of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:20, and “unto God and the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The six words of Moroni 4:2 that matter — ‘the Father in the name of’ — therefore have a single KJV address. John's related formula is different in shape: “the Father in my name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 15:16 and 16:23, and puts the possessive before ‘name’ rather than a genitive after it.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:20 is a thanksgiving formula, and it stands inside Paul's one sustained description of what a congregation does when it assembles — speaking in psalms and hymns, singing, giving thanks, submitting to one another (5:19-21). Moroni 4:2 is the rubric for exactly that moment: the congregation kneeling and the prayer beginning. Recover Ephesians 5:20's context and the sacrament prayer turns out to be introduced in the words the New Testament uses for congregational thanksgiving generally — which is what the Greek word behind ‘eucharist’ means, and what the prayer itself, a blessing over bread, is. The Book of Mormon reaches that convergence without the Greek.

links.note: ‘And they did kneel down with the church, and pray to the Father in the name of Christ, saying.’ Six consecutive words of this clause reproduce a KJV singleton, and the singleton is the KJV's one verse for addressing the Father in the name of Christ in an act of thanksgiving. Moroni compresses: Ephesians' ‘our Lord Jesus Christ’ becomes ‘Christ’, and the vocative is deferred to the next verse, where the full form returns as ‘O God, the Eternal Father … in the name of thy Son Jesus Christ’ — that is, God, the Father, and Jesus Christ in Ephesians 5:20's own order. The one element the KJV verse does not supply is ‘pray’ for ‘giving thanks’, and the asking half of the prayer is adjudicated separately at 4:3 from John 16:23. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; the case rests on the singleton, not the length.

links.text: And when he had thus spoken, he kneeled down, and prayed with them all.

provenance.other: “kneeled down, and prayed” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Luke 22:41 (Gethsemane, alone), Acts 9:40 (Peter at Tabitha's bier, having put everyone out) and Acts 20:36 (Paul at Miletus). Only the third has a congregation kneeling with the one who prays, and Acts 21:5 repeats it — ‘we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed’ — with wives and children present. “with the church” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 11:26 and 1 Corinthians 16:19, neither of them a scene of prayer.
provenance.significance: Kneeling is not the New Testament's default posture for corporate prayer and the KJV records it as a congregational act only in Acts. Both Acts scenes are farewells — Paul leaving elders he will not see again — which is also the situation of Moroni 4, a set of ordinances written down by the last man alive to perform them. And the adjacency is not only thematic: Moroni 3:1 is catalogued in this book against Acts 20:17, the verse that opens the same Miletus scene by calling the elders of the church. Moroni 3 takes the summoning of the elders from the head of that scene and Moroni 4 takes the kneeling from its foot, which is the strongest thing this row has going for it — the chapter before it was already reading Acts 20.

links.note: ‘They did kneel down with the church, and pray.’ The elements are the KJV's three: kneeling, praying, and the whole company doing it together, which the KJV assembles only at Acts 20:36 and 21:5. Recorded at moderate because each element is ordinary English and the clause reproduces no run — ‘kneel down’ in the infinitive occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Genesis 24:11's camels, which is filed in the register as the trap it is. What raises it above a guess is recurrence: the immediately preceding chapter borrows Acts 20:17 for its own opening clause (see Moroni 3:1), so the writer of this appendix demonstrably had that page of Acts in view nineteen verses earlier.
links.whyNot: ‘Kneel down and pray’ is a phrase any nineteenth-century writer describing a service could produce without a Bible open. There is no shared distinctive word and no shared syntax beyond the coordination of two ordinary verbs; if the row is wrong, it is wrong because a common posture has been mistaken for a borrowing.

pericopes.text: O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it, that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him, and keep his commandments which he hath given them, that they may always have his spirit to be with them. Amen.

links.text: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.

provenance.other: “in remembrance of me” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 — that is, in the two institution accounts that carry the remembrance command and nowhere else; Matthew and Mark do not have it. “this bread” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, three in John 6 and two in 1 Corinthians 11 (11:26, 11:27), and the Pauline pair are the ones about eating it in the assembly. “the body of Christ” occurs in exactly four KJV verses.
provenance.significance: Recover the context of 1 Corinthians 11:24 and what surrounds it is a warning: verses 27-29 make eating this bread unworthily a guilt and a damnation. Moroni's prayer takes the institution frame and replaces the warning with a covenant. Where Paul attaches a threat to the act (‘guilty of the body and blood of the Lord’), Moroni attaches three conditions and a promise — willing to take the name, always remember him, keep his commandments, that they may always have his Spirit. The negative sanction has not been dropped from the book; it is two chapters away at Moroni 6:1-4 and, verbatim from Paul, at 3 Nephi 18:29. What the prayer does is move the Pauline apparatus out of the words said over the bread and into the discipline around them, leaving the prayer itself entirely positive. That is a liturgical decision, and it is visible only against the KJV verse it declines to quote.

links.note: ‘To bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it, that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son.’ The remembrance command is the Lukan-Pauline layer of the institution and the Book of Mormon has already used it, at 3 Nephi 18:7, in Christ's own mouth; Moroni 4:3 is that layer fixed as a set prayer. The distinctive move, and it is the same one made at 3 Nephi 18:7, is that remembrance is attached to the body rather than to the person: the KJV predicates the body and then commands remembrance of *me* (‘this is my body … this do in remembrance of me’), while Moroni has them ‘eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son’. 1 Corinthians rather than Luke because Paul's is the repeatable ordinance text — ‘as often as ye eat this bread’ — where Luke's is narrative, and because ‘this bread’ is Paul's phrase for the element in the hands of a congregation. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; the run is short and the frame is what is borrowed.

links.text: And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

provenance.other: “ask the Father in my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 16:23. “the Father in my name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 15:16 and 16:23, and both are instructions about petition. The formula is exclusively Johannine; no other New Testament writer tells anyone to ask the Father in the Son's name.
provenance.significance: John 16:23 is an instruction with a guarantee attached — whatsoever ye shall ask, he will give it you. Moroni 4:3 is the instruction being carried out, and it is the only place in the Book of Mormon where the reader is given the fixed words of a prayer to perform rather than a report of one. So the metalepsis runs forward rather than back: what is suppressed is not the source's context but its promise. A congregation reciting this prayer is exercising a warrant printed elsewhere, and the prayer's confidence — it asks, it does not plead — is borrowed from a verse the prayer never cites.

links.note: ‘We ask thee in the name of thy Son Jesus Christ.’ The KJV's one verse for asking the Father in the Son's name is John 16:23, and the Book of Mormon has already delivered that verse twice — at 3 Nephi 18:20, in the same discourse that instituted this ordinance, and at Moroni 2:2 two chapters earlier, where the verb is 'call on' rather than 'ask'. Here the formula is neither reported nor commanded but spoken. Moroni converts the third-person instruction into a first-person performance and, because the speaker is now addressing the Father directly, replaces the object with a pronoun and the possessive with a genitive: ‘ask the Father in my name’ becomes ‘ask thee … in the name of thy Son’. Every element survives the conversion. This is a distinct claim from the Ephesians 5:20 link at 4:2 and the two should be read together: Ephesians supplies the wording of the address, John the warrant for the asking, and the prayer needs both because it is at once a thanksgiving and a petition.

links.text: And he that keepeth his commandments dwelleth in him, and he in him. And hereby we know that he abideth in us, by the Spirit which he hath given us.

provenance.route: 1 John 3:24, with John 14:15-17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “which he hath given us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:24, and the clause it completes is ‘by the Spirit which he hath given us’. “keep his commandments” occurs in exactly eighteen KJV verses; a search of the whole KJV for a verse containing both that phrase and the word ‘spirit’ returns none, so 1 John 3:24 — with the participial ‘he that keepeth his commandments’ — is the Bible's one place where commandment-keeping and the given Spirit stand in a single sentence as cause and evidence. From the other side, “abide with you for ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:16, and “he dwelleth with you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:17 — the two halves of the Comforter promise that John 14:15 makes conditional on keeping the commandments.
provenance.significance: The prayer's closing clause is its only promise, and it is built out of the two New Testament passages that make the Spirit the consequence of obedience rather than a gift of grace at large. What Moroni does to 1 John 3:24 is move the participle: in John what is ‘given’ is the Spirit, and commandment-keeping is the evidence that it was; in Moroni what is ‘given’ is the commandments, and the Spirit is what is ‘had’ as a result. One relative clause changes hands and the theology tightens — the Spirit stops being the proof of a relationship and becomes the wage of a condition. The 1830 reads ‘his spirit’ in lower case, as it does almost everywhere (241 lower-case ‘spirit’ against 35 capitals across the first edition, so this is compositor's practice and not a local judgment); 1920 capitalises it, and the effect, whatever the intention, is to make the phrase look like the KJV's ‘the Spirit which he hath given us’ in a way the first edition does not.

links.note: ‘Keep his commandments which he hath given them, that they may always have his spirit to be with them.’ Four words of that clause — ‘which he hath given’ plus a pronoun — reproduce a KJV singleton, and the singleton sits in the one verse of the Bible that connects keeping the commandments to possessing the Spirit. The sequence matches: commandments kept, then the Spirit had, then the abiding. John 14:15-17 supplies the durative that 1 John does not, ‘that he may abide with you for ever’ behind ‘that they may always have his Spirit to be with them’, and John 14 reaches it by the same route — ‘if ye love me, keep my commandments’, and the Father will give the Comforter. The Book of Mormon has fused the Johannine epistle's clause with the Johannine gospel's promise, which is unsurprising given that they are the closest things in the KJV to each other, and has made the fusion the last line of a prayer said every week.

pericopes.text: The manner of administering the wine. Behold, they took the cup, and said,

links.text: After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.

provenance.other: “took the cup” occurs in exactly 4 KJV verses — Matthew 26:27, Mark 14:23, Luke 22:17 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 — which is to say in the institution narrative and nowhere else. “after the same manner” occurs in exactly 4 KJV verses, of which 1 Corinthians 11:25 is the only one at the Lord's table.
provenance.significance: Recover the context of 1 Corinthians 11:25 and it is not narrative at all: Paul quotes the institution in the middle of correcting a congregation's practice — ‘when ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord's supper’ (11:20) — so the words are cited there as a rule of order, which is what makes them quotable as a rubric. Moroni 4-5 do exactly that and nothing else: two chapters of a dozen lines whose only business is to fix the wording, appended by a man who expects his church to be extinguished. The borrowing is of a genre as much as of a phrase, and the genre is Paul's, not the evangelists'.

links.note: ‘Behold, they took the cup, and said.’ The whole narrative frame of the wine chapter is four words of the institution narrative. “took the cup” occurs in exactly 4 KJV verses, and all four are the same moment, so the run by itself chooses no source. The chapter's own heading does. Moroni 4:1 announced ‘the manner of their elders and priests administering’; Moroni 5:1 answers ‘The manner of administering the wine’, and the one KJV verse that introduces the cup by looking back to the manner of the bread is Paul's — ‘After the same manner also he took the cup.’ The pairing of the two chapters is therefore not merely liturgical convenience; it reproduces the sequencing device of 1 Corinthians 11:23-25, where the cup is given as a repetition of what was just done with the bread. The 1830 punctuation makes this plainer than the current text: the first edition closes the heading as its own sentence, where 1920 runs it into the narrative with a dash, so 1830 shows Moroni 4 and 5 as a matched pair of rubrics and the modern text shows two sentences.
links.whyNot: The shared string is four words and they are the same four words in all four KJV institution accounts; ‘took the cup’ alone cannot identify a source, and the Pauline preference here rests on the ‘manner’ framing, which is an argument about the chapter's structure rather than about its wording. A reader who declines that argument still has a link to the institution narrative in general and should read this row at that level. Note also that the Book of Mormon has its own cup narrative at 3 Nephi 18:8-11, which Moroni 4:1 says the elders were obeying; ‘took the cup’ does not occur there, which is why this row points at the KJV rather than at 3 Nephi.

pericopes.text: O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee, in the name of thy Son Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this wine to the souls of all those who drink of it, that they may do it in remembrance of the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them, that they may witness unto thee, O God the Eternal Father, that they do always remember him, that they may have his spirit to be with them. Amen.

links.text: After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 11:25 / Luke 22:20 → KJV → 3 Nephi 18:11 → Moroni 5:2. The schema has no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage — `OT-via-earlier-BoM` covers only Old Testament sources — so `mediation` is recorded as `uncertain` and the route is given here rather than forced into an enum that cannot hold it. Flagged for CONVENTIONS §7: the field wants a sixth value, `NT-via-earlier-BoM`, and this adjudicator has not invented one.
provenance.other: “in remembrance of me” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 — and the first two attach the command to the bread. Only 1 Corinthians 11:25 extends it to the drinking, and its clause “as oft as ye drink” occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse. Matthew and Mark have no remembrance command at all. “do it in remembrance” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses; that exact wording is the Book of Mormon's own, at 3 Nephi 18:11.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 11:25 is the hinge of a passage about eating and drinking unworthily, and Paul's remedy four verses later is that a man examine himself. Moroni's prayer takes the remembrance clause and leaves the examination behind: it asks not that the communicants be found worthy but that they be given the Spirit. The conditions Paul makes a test survive in the pair of prayers only as things the communicants are ‘willing’ to do, and only over the bread (Moroni 4:3); over the wine they are dropped. Read against its source, the wine prayer is the institution with Paul's warning removed.

links.note: ‘to bless and sanctify this wine to the souls of all those who drink of it, that they may do it in remembrance of the blood of thy Son.’ A remembrance clause attached to the cup is a Pauline peculiarity, and nothing else in the KJV supplies it: “in remembrance of me” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses and only 1 Corinthians 11:25 puts the remembrance with the drinking rather than with the bread. The sequence of the prayer is that verse's sequence — the cup, the drinking of it, the remembrance — and the fact that a wine prayer has a remembrance clause at all is a fact about Paul, since Matthew and Mark give the cup no such command. The proximate wording, however, is the Book of Mormon's own: ‘ye shall do it in remembrance of my blood’ stands at 3 Nephi 18:11, adjudicated in this catalogue to Luke 22:20 with 1 Corinthians 11:25 composite, and Moroni 5:2 is that sentence put into the third person and into a prayer. The link is written here rather than deferred because a new book is a new hand and a reader of Moroni is shown Moroni's page (ADJUDICATING §4).
links.whyNot: Every distinctive word of this clause already stands at 3 Nephi 18:11, where the risen Christ institutes the ordinance that Moroni 4:1 says the elders administered ‘according to the commandments of Christ’. A reader could reasonably hold that Moroni 5:2 borrows from 3 Nephi and from nothing else, and that the Pauline contact is inherited rather than fresh. The row is kept because the prayer is demonstrably not a transcript of 3 Nephi 18:11 — see the Luke 22:20 row at this verse for the word where it moves back toward the KJV — and because the mediation cannot be recorded honestly in the present enum; see `provenance.route`.

links.text: Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 11:25 / Luke 22:20 → KJV → 3 Nephi 18:11 → Moroni 5:2. The schema has no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage — `OT-via-earlier-BoM` covers only Old Testament sources — so `mediation` is recorded as `uncertain` and the route is given here rather than forced into an enum that cannot hold it. Flagged for CONVENTIONS §7: the field wants a sixth value, `NT-via-earlier-BoM`, and this adjudicator has not invented one.
provenance.other: “which is shed for” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses. Matthew 26:28 and Mark 14:24 read ‘shed for many’ — “shed for many” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses — and Luke 22:20 reads ‘shed for you’, which occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse. “the new testament in my blood” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25, and neither Moroni prayer uses it.
provenance.significance: The one thing Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 both say about the cup, and say in the same seven words, is that it is the new testament in the speaker's blood. Both Moroni prayers take everything around that clause and leave the clause itself. The covenant language is not lost: it is relocated to the bread, where the communicants ‘are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son’ (Moroni 4:3). So the pair redistributes the institution — covenant with the body, memory with the blood — where the KJV puts the covenant with the cup and, in Luke and Paul both, the memory with the bread. That inversion is the substantive departure of Moroni 4-5 from their source, and it is visible only when the two chapters are read as the single rubric they are.

links.note: ‘in remembrance of the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them.’ The atonement clause of the wine prayer takes Luke's side of a split in the KJV institution accounts: “shed for you” occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Luke 22:20, against Matthew 26:28 and Mark 14:24's ‘shed for many’. The Book of Mormon takes that side twice. At 3 Nephi 18:11 the risen Christ says ‘my blood, which I have shed for you’, converting Luke's present passive into an active perfect a speaker on the far side of the crucifixion needs. Here the elders convert it again — into the third person, and back into the passive: ‘the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them’. The second conversion is the one worth noticing, because a prayer about the congregation did not require a passive at all; ‘which he hath shed for them’ would have followed 3 Nephi's grammar exactly and did not happen. What appears instead is the KJV's voice with Luke's preposition, which is some evidence that the prayer was set against its biblical source and not only copied from the Nephite one. Neither Matthew's ‘many’ nor his ‘for the remission of sins’ appears anywhere in either prayer.
links.whyNot: The passive may be nothing more than what the third person made convenient, and the move from ‘you’ to ‘them’ is forced by the fact that the elders pray about the congregation rather than to it — so the grammatical argument for a fresh look at Luke 22:20 is suggestive, not decisive. What is not in doubt is that the clause is Lukan rather than Matthean in shape; what is arguable is whether Moroni 5:2 reaches Luke through 3 Nephi 18:11 alone. The mediation is recorded as `uncertain` for that reason and the route is spelled out in `provenance.route`.

pericopes.text: And now I speak concerning baptism. Behold, elders, priests, and teachers were baptized; and they were not baptized, save they brought forth fruit meet that they were worthy of it;

links.text: Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:

provenance.route: Matthew 3:8, conflated with Luke 3:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “fruits meet for repentance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:8; “worthy of repentance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 3:8. The two are the Synoptic variants of one saying of John the Baptist, and “Bring forth therefore fruits” is the four words they share. Inside the Book of Mormon “fruit meet” occurs only here; Alma 5:54 has the Matthean form entire (“bring forth fruit meet for repentance”) and nothing else in the book has either.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowed words are the Baptist's, spoken at the Jordan to men presenting themselves for baptism — the one place in the Gospels where a qualification is imposed on candidates before the water. Moroni 6:1 is imposing exactly that qualification on Nephite candidates, and it takes the words from the scene that invented the problem. The suppressed half is what follows in both Synoptics: the axe laid to the root, and the warning that descent from Abraham confers nothing. A church whose membership is about to be annihilated is defining membership by the saying that denies membership can be inherited.

links.note: 'And they were not baptized, save they brought forth fruit meet that they were worthy of it.' The clause holds both Synoptic forms of one verse at once: 'fruit meet' is Matthew's word (KJV 'meet', for the Greek ἄξιος) and 'worthy' is Luke's rendering of the same word, and Moroni has them side by side in a sentence neither Gospel could produce alone. That conflation is the argument for the KJV rather than for Alma 5:54 as the proximate model — Alma reproduces Matthew's phrase intact and does not touch Luke's, so a writer copying Alma would have had no occasion to reach for 'worthy'. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six. Note also what the borrowing does to the grammar: the KJV's fruits are meet *for repentance*, an abstract standard; Moroni's are meet *that they were worthy of it*, i.e. of baptism, and the standard has been transferred from the disposition to the ordinance.

pericopes.text: neither did they receive any unto baptism, save they came forth with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, and witnessed unto the church that they truly repented of all their sins.

links.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

provenance.other: “a broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 34:18, and “a contrite spirit” in exactly two, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2. Psalm 34:18 is therefore the only verse in the King James Bible that pairs the two nouns in Moroni's order and in Moroni's grammar. Psalm 51:17 has both words but redistributed — 'a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart' — and mediation-check.py against Isaiah 66:2 returns the Psalm 34:18 form as decisive on the surviving backbone.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 51:17, if the pairing is thought to come from the penitential psalm rather than from Psalm 34; the noun-adjective distribution is against it.
provenance.significance: Psalm 34 is the psalm of the man who feigned madness before Abimelech and got away, and its promise is proximity — the LORD is *nigh* to the broken-hearted. Moroni's clause turns the promise into a threshold: what the psalm says God draws near to, the Nephite church requires before it will admit anyone. The nearness that was gratuitous in the source has become a condition in the borrowing.

links.note: The phrase is the Book of Mormon's settled baptismal formula and Moroni is at the end of a chain, not the start of one: 2 Nephi 2:7 has it first, and 3 Nephi 9:20 puts it in the mouth of the risen Christ as the sacrifice that replaces burnt offering — 'ye shall offer for a sacrifice unto me a broken heart and a contrite spirit'. Moroni 6:2 is a church-order rubric written by a man whose own record contains that commandment four chapters' distance away, so the proximate model is the Nephite Christ and not the psalter; the KJV wording behind both is Psalm 34:18's, unaltered. Catalogued here rather than passed over because Moroni is a new book in a new hand (ADJUDICATING §4), and a reader of Moroni 6 shown nothing at this verse would be told there is no borrowing in it.

pericopes.text: And none were received unto baptism, save they took upon them the name of Christ, having a determination to serve him unto the end.

And after that they had been received unto the baptism, and were wrought upon and cleansed by the power of the Holy Ghost, they were numbered among the people of the church of Christ, and their names were taken, that they might be remembered and nourished by the good word of God, to keep them in the right way, to keep them continually watchful unto prayer, relying alone upon the merits of Christ, who was the author and the finisher of their faith.

links.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

provenance.other: “author and finisher” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 12:2, and the pairing occurs nowhere else in English scripture. Inside the Book of Mormon “author and the finisher” occurs once, here.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 12:1-2 is a race run 'with patience' by men 'compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses'. Moroni 6 is a chapter of witnesses — the candidate witnesses to the church at 6:2, three witnesses condemn at 6:7 — and of members kept 'in the right way' and 'continually watchful'. Recover the context and the borrowed title supplies the metaphor the whole chapter is administering: the church's business is keeping people in a race whose finisher is Christ. The suppressed clause is the next one, that he 'endured the cross, despising the shame' — which is what Moroni's own situation asks of the last members of a church being destroyed.

links.note: Six words in order from a KJV singleton, altered only by an inserted article and a change of possessive: Hebrews' 'the author and finisher of our faith' becomes 'the author and the finisher of their faith'. Dependence is not seriously deniable; nothing else in English scripture calls Christ this. The 1830 reads 'who was the author and the finisher of their faith' — the extra 'the' is the first edition's and survives into the current text, so this is one of the rare places where 1830 is *further* from the KJV than a modern reader would guess. The surrounding clause 'relying alone upon the merits of Christ' has no KJV background at all: 'merit' in any form is not a King James word, and the sentence is therefore half borrowed diction and half a vocabulary the KJV does not possess. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

links.text: But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.

provenance.other: “watch unto prayer” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 4:7; the fuller “sober and watch” run is a singleton in the same verse. Inside the Book of Mormon “watchful unto prayer” occurs twice, at Alma 34:39 and here, and the adverb travels with it both times — Amulek's 'watchful unto prayer continually', Moroni's 'continually watchful unto prayer'.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter's clause is eschatological before it is devotional: the reason to watch unto prayer is that 'the end of all things is at hand'. Moroni is writing after the end of all things has in fact come for his nation. The catalogue's charge to keep members 'continually watchful unto prayer' is being recorded by the one survivor of the church that failed to be.

links.note: A KJV singleton reversed but intact. The catalogue adjudicated 1 Peter 4:7 at Alma 34:39, where Amulek uses it in an exhortation against temptation; here it has become an item in a church's standing duty of care toward new members, which is a different use of the same three words and the reason it is written as a fresh link rather than a repeat (ADJUDICATING §4 — a new book, a new hand). The word order is inverted in both Nephite occurrences, and the adverb 'continually' is common to both and absent from Peter, which suggests Moroni has the Alma passage in his ear rather than the epistle; the KJV wording behind either is Peter's. The schema has no mediation value for an NT source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage, so this row is marked direct-NT and the route field carries the argument.

links.text: And have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come,

provenance.route: Hebrews 6:5, with the verb of 1 Timothy 4:6 → KJV → Jacob 6:7 → Moroni 6:4
provenance.other: “the good word of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:5, where the verb is 'tasted'. “nourished up” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which only 1 Timothy 4:6 nourishes anybody on words — 'nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine'. Inside the Book of Mormon 'nourished by the good word of God' occurs twice, at Jacob 6:7 and here, verbatim.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 6:4-6 is the passage on those who, having tasted the good word of God, fall away and cannot be renewed to repentance — the New Testament's hardest saying about apostasy. Moroni 6 is a chapter whose next paragraph blots names out of the register. The good word by which members are nourished at 6:4 comes from the one KJV verse where tasting it does not guarantee that they stay.

links.note: The catalogue adjudicated Hebrews 6:5 at Jacob 6:7, which has this clause word for word, so the phrase enters the Book of Mormon long before Moroni and enters it already fused: the KJV's verb is 'tasted', not 'nourished', and the substitution is the Nephite formula's, not Moroni's. Written here rather than passed over because Moroni is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4), and downgraded to moderate because what Moroni is most plausibly reproducing is Jacob's sentence rather than Hebrews'. 1 Timothy 4:6 is offered as the source of the verb and no more than that — it is the only KJV verse that nourishes a person on words — and a reader who thinks 'nourished' is simply the natural English for feeding on a word should decline that half. The schema has no mediation value for an NT source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage; direct-NT plus the route field is doing that work.

pericopes.text: And the church did meet together oft, to fast and to pray, and to speak one with another concerning the welfare of their souls;

links.text: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.

provenance.route: Acts 2:42 and 2:46 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: No distinctive string is shared. “continued stedfastly” is a KJV singleton at Acts 2:42 and does not appear in the Book of Mormon at all. What is shared is the inventory: habitual assembly, prayer, mutual speech, and the breaking of bread, in that order across Moroni 6:5-6 as across Acts 2:42 and 2:46.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:41-47 is the New Testament's only sustained description of what a newly baptized church actually did, and it is introduced by a mass baptism and a count of those 'added unto them' — which is Moroni 6:1-4's subject, down to the taking of names. Moroni 6 reads as the Nephite answer to that paragraph, and the two verses stand at the same point in the same sequence.

links.note: Moroni 6:5-6 is not verbally dependent on Acts 2 and the row is offered as form, not wording. But the correspondence is unusually complete: Acts 2 moves baptism → those added were numbered → continuing in doctrine and fellowship → breaking of bread → prayers → daily assembly; Moroni 6 moves baptism → 'they were numbered among the people of the church' → meeting together oft → fasting and prayer → speaking one with another → meeting together oft to partake of bread and wine. Two paragraphs written to answer the same question could arrive independently at the same list of activities, which is why this is moderate rather than high; what they are less likely to do independently is arrive at it in the same order and in the same position after a baptismal narrative. 'To fast and to pray' is not from Acts 2, which never fasts; the nearest KJV settings are Acts 13:3 and 14:23, and 14:23 is already in this book's apparatus at Moroni 3:2.
links.whyNot: There is not one distinctive shared word. Every element of the correspondence is a thing any assembling congregation does, and a writer describing a church at all would have to mention meeting, praying and the sacrament in some order. A reader who holds that the parallel is generated by the subject matter rather than by the text has nothing verbal to answer.

links.text: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.

provenance.route: Hebrews 10:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon, if at all
provenance.other: “assembling of ourselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 10:25. The word does not occur in Moroni 6, which says 'did meet together oft' instead; the only lexical contact is 'together' and the exhorting of 6:9.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 10:25 is the one verse in the Bible that makes frequency of assembly a commandment and neglect of it a named fault. If it stands behind Moroni 6:5-6, then the repeated 'oft' — twice in two verses, and unusual emphasis for a chapter otherwise so compressed — is answering Hebrews' 'so much the more, as ye see the day approaching', and the church's diligence is being measured against an approaching end that Moroni, alone of all writers, has already watched arrive.

links.note: Recorded because Hebrews 10:25 is where a reader will look for this chapter's background and the catalogue should say what it found there. The doubled 'oft' at 6:5 and 6:6 is the feature that wants explaining: the chapter is otherwise terse, and it says twice in successive clauses that the church met together often, which is an emphasis rather than a description. Hebrews 10:25 is the only KJV verse that supplies a reason for that emphasis.
links.whyNot: No shared wording of any kind. The KJV's 'assembling' and 'forsaking' are both absent, and 'meet together oft' is the Nephite formula already fixed at 3 Nephi 18:22, where the risen Christ commands it — which supplies the doubled 'oft' internally and leaves Hebrews with nothing to do. Withdraw this row if 3 Nephi 18:22 is judged sufficient, which it may well be.

pericopes.text: and they did meet together oft to partake of bread and wine, in remembrance of the Lord Jesus;

links.text: After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.

provenance.other: “as oft as” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 4:8 and 1 Corinthians 11:25; only the Pauline one is sacramental. “in remembrance of me” occurs in exactly three, Luke 22:19 and 1 Corinthians 11:24 and 11:25 — the institution narrative and Paul's citation of it. “the Lord Jesus the same night” is a singleton at 1 Corinthians 11:23. Inside the Book of Mormon 'in remembrance of the Lord Jesus' occurs once, here.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 11 is the only place in the New Testament where the Lord's Supper is legislated rather than narrated: Paul gives the words of institution in order to correct how a congregation is keeping them, and follows with unworthy partaking, self-examination and judgment. Moroni 6 has just given the words of institution itself, at chapters 4 and 5, and 6:6 is the rubric of frequency that Paul's chapter is arguing about. The suppressed half is 11:27-29 — that a man eat and drink damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body — which is precisely the anxiety governing 6:7's discipline two verses later.

links.note: 'And they did meet together oft to partake of bread and wine, in remembrance of the Lord Jesus.' Three of Paul's distinctive markers are here in one clause: the adverb of frequency ('oft', which is 1 Corinthians 11:25's own word and not Luke's), the purpose ('in remembrance of'), and the title 'the Lord Jesus', which is 11:23's designation of the one who instituted the rite. The verse follows the two sacrament prayers of Moroni 4 and 5, so it is the frequency rubric appended to an institution formula — Paul's own arrangement. Against Luke 22:19, which supplies 'in remembrance of me' but nothing else, the 'oft' is decisive: Luke has no adverb of frequency. Against 3 Nephi 18:22, which fixes 'meet together oft' as the Nephite formula, the phrase 'in remembrance of the Lord Jesus' is what remains Pauline — 3 Nephi 18 has 'in remembrance of my body' and 'of my blood', never the title. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six. The 1830 'bread and wine' is worth flagging: the KJV's element is 'the cup', and later Latter-day Saint practice replaced the wine, so the first edition preserves the sacramental substance Paul assumes.

pericopes.text: and they were strict to observe that there should be no iniquity among them; and whoso was found to commit iniquity, and three witnesses of the church did condemn them before the elders; and if they repented not, and confessed not, their names were blotted out, and they were not numbered among the people of Christ;

links.text: But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 19:15 → Matthew 18:16-17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “two or three witnesses” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all of them New Testament citations of Deuteronomy: Matthew 18:16, 2 Corinthians 13:1, 1 Timothy 5:19, Hebrews 10:28. The Deuteronomic original reads 'at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses' (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare 17:6). Moroni has neither form — he has three witnesses flat, with no 'two or', which is why the mediation is argued from sequence rather than from wording. mediation-check.py against Deuteronomy 19:15 and Matthew 18:16 returns no decisive point in either direction.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:15-17 is the New Testament's only procedure for excluding a member, and its last step is the church: 'tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.' Moroni's witnesses are 'three witnesses of the church', and what follows non-repentance is that the offender is 'not numbered among the people of Christ' — Matthew's heathen man, in Nephite bookkeeping.

links.note: The verse runs Matthew 18's procedure in Matthew 18's order: offence, witnesses, the church, and on refusal to repent, exclusion. Where it departs is instructive. Moroni requires three witnesses and not Matthew's 'two or three', which is a hardening of the rule and cannot come from any KJV verse — every biblical formulation admits two. And the witnesses in Moroni are officers of the church who condemn 'before the elders', where in Matthew they are companions brought along by the offended party. So this is the Matthean procedure administered by an institution that Matthew's text does not yet have. Catalogued as an allusion at moderate rather than high precisely because the wording will not carry it: the case is sequence and setting, and a reader who thinks any church devising a discipline would arrive at witnesses and elders has a fair objection. Mediation is called OT-via-NT because the witness rule is Deuteronomy's and every English form of it that Moroni could be following is a New Testament one.
