links.text: He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.

provenance.other: “blot out his name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 29:20 and Revelation 3:5; only Revelation's is a register of members. Exodus 32:33 has 'him will I blot out of my book'. Inside the Book of Mormon 'their names were blotted out' occurs four times — Mosiah 26:36, Alma 1:24, Alma 6:3 and here — and the catalogue adjudicated Revelation 3:5 at Mosiah 26:36.
provenance.significance: Revelation 3:5 is a promise, not a threat: the overcomer is the one whose name will *not* be blotted out. Moroni's church performs the operation the risen Christ promises to withhold, which makes the borrowing an unusually exact piece of metalepsis — the phrase carries its own negation with it, and the reader who recovers Revelation 3:5 is being told what the Nephite elders' act imitates and what it cannot do. The register of the church is not the book of life; the same verb governs both.

links.note: This verse and 6:4 are a pair, and the pair is the argument. At 6:4 'their names were taken, that they might be remembered'; at 6:7 'their names were blotted out'. A register in which names are written and struck is the book of life of Revelation 3:5 and Exodus 32:33 made administrative, and the Book of Mormon has run the formula that way since Mosiah 26:36 — where Alma's revelation produces the identical sentence, 'the same were not numbered among the people of the church, and their names were blotted out'. Moroni 6:7 reproduces that Nephite sentence almost exactly, changing 'the church' to 'Christ'. So the proximate model is internal and the KJV wording behind it is Revelation's; the schema has no mediation value for that route and direct-NT with the route field is standing in. Written as a link rather than a cross-reference because Moroni is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4).

pericopes.text: but as oft as they repented, and sought forgiveness, with real intent, they were forgiven.

links.text: Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?

provenance.route: Matthew 18:21-22, with Luke 17:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “how oft” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Job 21:17, Psalm 78:40 and Matthew 18:21; only Matthew's is about repeated forgiveness. “seventy times seven” is a KJV singleton at Matthew 18:22. Luke 17:4 states the same rule with the repetition attached to the offender's repentance — 'seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him' — which is Moroni's construction, where the frequency belongs to the repenting and not to the forgiving.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:21 is Peter's question about the limit of forgiveness and it comes four verses after the discipline procedure of 18:15-17. Moroni 6:8 is the answer to the same question and it comes one verse after his discipline procedure. The suppressed half is the parable that follows in Matthew, the servant forgiven a debt who will not forgive one — a story about a man restored to a community he then fails.

links.note: The row rests on adjacency, not on wording, and it is written because the adjacency is exact. Moroni 6:7 runs the procedure of Matthew 18:15-17 (see the link at that verse); Moroni 6:8 then supplies the qualification that in Matthew comes at 18:21-22 — that there is no limit on how often a penitent may be received back. 'As oft as they repented … they were forgiven' is Luke 17:4's construction rather than Matthew's, with the frequency attached to the repentance; the two Synoptic forms are as close together here as they were at 6:1, where Matthew and Luke's versions of the Baptist's saying were conflated in one clause. That recurring habit within a single chapter is the strongest thing this row has. 'With real intent' is not from either Gospel — it is the Nephite phrase fixed at 2 Nephi 31:13 and used four times in Moroni's own pages.
links.whyNot: There is no distinctive shared string: 'as oft as' is Pauline in the KJV, not Matthean, and 'how oft', 'seventy times seven' and 'trespass against thee' are all absent from Moroni 6:8. The case is entirely that Moroni's two verses stand in the order Matthew's two paragraphs stand in, and a chapter on church discipline would in any case have to say both things.

pericopes.text: And their meetings were conducted by the church, after the manner of the workings of the spirit, and by the power of the Holy Ghost: for as the power of the Holy Ghost led them whether to preach, or exhort, or to pray, or to supplicate, or to sing, even so it was done.

links.text: What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 12 and 14 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “pray with the spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “sing with the spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them 1 Corinthians 14:15, which is the only verse in the Bible that pairs praying and singing as things done by the Spirit. “severally as he will” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:11 ('all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will'); “diversities of operations” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:6; “decently and in order” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 14:40.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 12-14 is the New Testament's only regulation of a meeting conducted by the Spirit rather than by an order of service, and 14:26 is its inventory — 'when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation'. Moroni's five verbs are that inventory turned into verbs. The unstated correspondence is Paul's whole anxiety, that a meeting run by the Spirit will run to disorder, answered in 14:40 by 'let all things be done decently and in order' — which is the clause Moroni's closing 'even so it was done' rewrites into obedience. In Corinth the Spirit's freedom was a problem to be governed; in Moroni it is the government.

links.note: 'For as the power of the Holy Ghost led them whether to preach, or exhort, or to pray, or to supplicate, or to sing, even so it was done.' Praying and singing are the two items Paul pairs at 14:15 as done 'with the spirit', and they are the two items in Moroni's list of five that the KJV supplies with the same qualification; exhorting is Romans 12:8's word ('he that exhorteth, on exhortation'), while preaching and supplication belong to neither list and are Moroni's own. The framing clause is 1 Corinthians 12's rather than 14's: 'after the manner of the workings of the spirit' answers 'diversities of operations' (12:6) and 'the power of the Holy Ghost led them … even so it was done' answers the Spirit 'dividing to every man severally as he will' (12:11). What Moroni does with the material is invert its purpose. Paul writes chapters 12 and 14 to *restrain* a spirit-led meeting; Moroni reports a spirit-led meeting as the Nephite norm, with the same vocabulary and none of the anxiety. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And now I, Moroni, write a few of the words of my father Mormon, which he spake concerning faith, hope and charity: for after this manner did he speak unto the people, as he taught them in the synagogue which they had built for the place of worship.

provenance.other: “faith, hope, charity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni inserts the conjunction — “faith, hope and charity” — but the three terms and their order are the KJV's, and 'charity' rather than 'love' is the King James translators' word at this verse.
provenance.significance: This is a table of contents written out of a single Pauline verse, and the sermon then obeys it. Faith is treated at 7:21-39, hope at 7:40-43, charity at 7:44-48, in Paul's order and with no fourth term; the chapter reaches 1 Corinthians 13 itself only at 7:45, forty-four verses after the triad has silently set its shape. Recovering Paul's context supplies what Moroni's heading suppresses: 13:13 is a ranking as well as a list, 'but the greatest of these is charity', and the sermon's structure is an argument that the ranking is right. Mormon's charity section is last because Paul's is greatest.

links.note: “A few of the words of my father Mormon, which he spake concerning faith, hope and charity.” The heading of the chapter is the KJV's one occurrence of the triad, and the interest is not the borrowing but what is done with it: the triad supplies the outline of a sermon that will not quote its source until verse 45. The same three words in the same order stand at Alma 7:24 and Ether 12:28, so this is the corpus's third use of 1 Corinthians 13:13 and its most structural. Moroni supplies the frame in his own voice — he is quoting his father — which means the Pauline triad has been carried across two authorial hands before Paul is reached.
links.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

pericopes.text: And now I, Mormon, speak unto you, my beloved brethren; and it is by the grace of God, the Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, and his holy will, because of the gift of his calling unto me, that I am permitted to speak unto you at this time;

provenance.other: “the gift of the grace of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “gifts and calling” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:29, which is the other half of Mormon's compound: he has a gift, a calling, and a grace, and the KJV joins gift to grace once and gift to calling once.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 3:7 is Paul accounting for his standing to speak to a congregation that is not his by birth — 'whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me'. Mormon opens a synagogue sermon by accounting for his standing in the same terms and with the same modesty formula, 'that I am permitted to speak unto you at this time'. The suppressed correspondence is the situation, not the sentence: an outsider's warrant to preach.

links.note: “It is by the grace of God, the Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, and his holy will, because of the gift of his calling unto me, that I am permitted to speak unto you.” Held at moderate and typed as an echo because no clause is reproduced: what Mormon has is the KJV's two rare collocations of gift with grace and gift with calling, redistributed into one sentence of his own construction. The machine's proposal here was 1 Thessalonians 3:11, on the six-word run 'and our Lord Jesus Christ' preceded by 'Father'; that is the KJV's standing epistolary salutation and is excluded in the register.
links.text: Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power.

pericopes.text: wherefore I would speak unto you that are of the church, that are the peaceable followers of Christ, and that have obtained a sufficient hope, by which ye can enter into the rest of the Lord, from this time hence forth, until ye shall rest with him in Heaven.

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11 → Hebrews 3:11-4:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “into his rest” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Hebrews 3:18, 4:1 and 4:10, all inside the one argument; the Psalm's own form is 'into my rest', spoken by God in the first person. Moroni 7:3 has neither pronoun but 'the rest of the Lord', which is the third-person form an expositor uses and which the Book of Mormon has used at Alma 12:36, 13:12, 13:16, 16:17 and 60:13.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 4:3 makes belief the condition of entry — 'we which have believed do enter into rest' — and Moroni 7:3 makes hope the condition: 'that have obtained a sufficient hope, by which ye can enter into the rest of the Lord'. The substitution is the sermon's programme in miniature, since the chapter's second section will argue that hope is what faith becomes (7:40-42). Recovering the source's context supplies the warning Mormon omits: Hebrews reaches the rest through a generation that failed to enter it, and Mormon addresses instead 'the peaceable followers of Christ', for whom the question is already settled.

links.note: “That have obtained a sufficient hope, by which ye can enter into the rest of the Lord, from this time hence forth, until ye shall rest with him in Heaven.” The mediation was settled two books ago and this row follows it: at Alma 12:33 the catalogue found the Psalm-or-Hebrews question decidable and decided for Hebrews, and nothing here reverses that. mediation-check.py returns one 'decisive' point for the Psalm at this verse, and it should be discounted — the point is that Moroni lacks Hebrews 4:3's trailing clause about the works finished from the foundation of the world, which is an absence, and an absence in a five-word paraphrase is not evidence. What decides is that the Book of Mormon's whole vocabulary of entering a divine rest is third-person expository ('the rest of the Lord'), which is the register of Hebrews' argument and not of the Psalm's oath. The 1830's 'from this time hence forth' was closed up to 'henceforth' in 1920.
links.text: For we which have believed do enter into rest, as he said, As I have sworn in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest: although the works were finished from the foundation of the world.

pericopes.text: And now my brethren, I judge these things of you because of your peaceable walk with the children of men:
for I remember the word of God, which saith, By their works ye shall know them: for if their works be good, then they are good also.

provenance.other: “by their fruits ye shall know them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “ye shall know them” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 7:16 and 7:20, which are the two ends of the same paragraph. Moroni's word order — preposition first — is 7:20's, not 7:16's.
provenance.significance: One word is changed and it changes the argument. Matthew's test is fruits, a metaphor with a tree behind it; Mormon's test is works, and works is the term the rest of his paragraph needs, because 7:6-10 is about gifts offered and prayers made rather than about anything that grows. The substitution is also what lets 7:11 keep the botanical figure and change the plant: Matthew's good tree becomes a bitter fountain, so the metaphor Mormon has just discarded returns six verses later in a form he has borrowed from elsewhere. Note too that the Book of Mormon already contains Matthew 7:20 verbatim, in Christ's mouth at 3 Nephi 14:20, with 'fruits' intact; Mormon, citing 'the word of God, which saith', quotes it wrong on purpose.

links.note: “For I remember the word of God, which saith, By their works ye shall know them: for if their works be good, then they are good also.” A citation formula followed by the KJV's one occurrence of the clause with a single lexical substitution, works for fruits, and then by Matthew 7:17's consequent ('a good tree bringeth forth good fruit') in the same substituted register. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the citation formula and the singleton: Mormon says he is quoting, and what he then produces is a KJV verse with one word moved. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 7:20 at this verse.
links.text: Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.

pericopes.text: For behold, God hath said, A man being evil, cannot do that which is good: for if he offereth a gift, or prayeth unto God, except he shall do it with real intent, it profiteth him nothing.

provenance.other: “profiteth me nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni's clause changes only the pronoun — 'it profiteth him nothing' — as the shift from Paul's first person to Mormon's third requires, and repeats it at 7:9.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's first contact with 1 Corinthians 13 and it happens thirty-nine verses before the chapter admits it. Paul's sentence is a gift given without charity: 'though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor … and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing'. Mormon's is a gift given without real intent. He has taken Paul's test and replaced Paul's term with his own, and the sermon will spend the next forty verses working back to the word he left out — arriving at 7:44, 'if he have not charity, he is nothing', which is Paul's other refrain from the same three verses. Read forward, 7:6 is a promissory note that 7:44-46 pays.

links.note: “If he offereth a gift, or prayeth unto God, except he shall do it with real intent, it profiteth him nothing.” The KJV's one occurrence of the clause, with the pronoun the new subject requires, in a sentence about the same subject as its source — a costly religious act voided by the disposition behind it. 'Real intent' stands where Paul has 'charity' and is the Book of Mormon's own phrase, at 2 Nephi 31:13, Moroni 6:8, here, 7:9 and 10:4. Hardy's apparatus cross-references 1 Corinthians 13:3 at this verse.
links.text: And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.

pericopes.text: For behold, it is not counted unto him for righteousness.

provenance.route: Genesis 15:6 → Romans 4:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “counted unto him for righteousness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 106:31 and Romans 4:3. Genesis 15:6, the verse Romans is quoting, reads 'he counted it to him for righteousness' — 'it to' where the New Testament has 'unto'. Moroni 7:7 has the New Testament's preposition.
provenance.significance: The mediation is decidable and it decides for Romans, which is also where the argument is. Genesis 15:6 is a narrative report about Abraham; Psalm 106:31 is the same formula applied to Phinehas's zeal, that is, to an act. Romans 4 is the one place in the KJV where the formula becomes a rule about what does and does not earn the reckoning, and Romans 4:5 states it in exactly Mormon's terms: 'to him that worketh not, but believeth'. Mormon's paragraph is a Nephite instance of Paul's argument — a man performs the outward act, the reckoning is withheld, and what is missing is the disposition.

links.note: “For behold, it is not counted unto him for righteousness.” Five words of a phrase the KJV has twice, in the form the New Testament gives it rather than the form Genesis gives it, attached to Romans 4's question rather than to Genesis's narrative or the Psalm's. mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence here, because the interpolated 'not' throws its alignment off the one word that settles the case; the preposition is decisive by eye, and CONVENTIONS §7 asks for a decision rather than a default. Held at high rather than certain because the phrase is a fixed formula and a writer steeped in the KJV could reach it without reaching for Romans.
links.text: For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.

pericopes.text: For behold, if a man being evil, giveth a gift, he doeth it grudgingly; wherefore it is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift; wherefore he is counted evil before God.

provenance.other: “grudgingly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is about the giving of a gift.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a rule for donors: 'Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.' Mormon supplies the verdict Paul leaves implied — the grudging gift is 'counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift', that is, the donor is treated as though he had never given. Recovering Paul's context also supplies the phrase 'as he purposeth in his heart', which is Mormon's 'real intent of heart' at 7:9 in different English; so the two halves of Mormon's paragraph, intent and grudging, are the two halves of one KJV verse.

links.note: “If a man being evil, giveth a gift, he doeth it grudgingly; wherefore it is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift.” A single word, but a word the King James Bible uses once, in the one place it legislates about the spirit in which a gift is made, inside a Book of Mormon paragraph about exactly that. Typed as an allusion rather than an echo because the shared item is not merely rare but situationally exact: the KJV's only grudging man is a donor, and so is Mormon's.
links.text: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

pericopes.text: And likewise also is it counted evil unto a man, if he shall pray, and not with real intent of heart; yea, and it profiteth him nothing: for God receiveth none such;
wherefore, a man being evil, cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift.

provenance.other: “being evil” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 7:11, Matthew 12:34 and Luke 11:13; “good gifts” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 7:11 and its Lukan parallel. Matthew 7:11 is the only KJV verse that holds both, and it stands in the same chapter as the fruits test Mormon quoted at 7:5 and the judgment rule he will quote at 7:18.
provenance.significance: Mormon contradicts his source, and the contradiction is the point. Matthew 7:11 concedes that evil men do give good gifts — 'If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children' — and uses the concession as the minor premise of an a fortiori about the Father. Moroni 7:10 denies it flatly: 'a man being evil, cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift.' The suppressed correspondence is what Matthew's argument was for. Jesus's point was that even bad fathers manage generosity, so God's must exceed it; Mormon's paragraph has already redefined a gift by its intent (7:6-8), which is what allows him to say that what an evil man hands over is not a gift at all. Matthew 12:34, the other 'being evil' verse, sits between a tree-and-fruit saying and a good-treasure saying and is the same argument in the Synoptic register.

links.note: “A man being evil, cannot do that which is good; neither will he give a good gift.” Two of Matthew 7:11's distinctive items in one clause, with the concessive turned into a denial. This is the second of three visits Mormon's discourse pays to Matthew 7 — 7:5 takes verse 20, this takes verse 11, 7:18 takes verse 2 — which is why the individual contacts should not be weighed one at a time: a chapter that quotes three separate verses of one Gospel chapter in twelve verses is working from that chapter. 'A man being evil' is Mormon's own refrain, at 7:6, 7:10 and again in 7:11's fountain.
links.text: If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?

pericopes.text: For behold, a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water; wherefore a man being the servant of the Devil, cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ, he cannot be a servant of the Devil.

provenance.route: James 3:11-12 + Matthew 7:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “cannot bring forth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:18, where the object is 'evil fruit'. The bitter-and-sweet water and the impossibility of one spring yielding both are James 3:11-12 and are in no other KJV passage.
provenance.significance: The verse is a graft, and the two stocks are visible. Matthew 7:18 supplies the syntax — a negated potential with a chiastic reversal, 'A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit' — and James 3:11-12 supplies the vehicle, the fountain that cannot yield both bitter and sweet. Mormon puts James's fountain inside Matthew's sentence: 'a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water.' This is why 7:5 could afford to lose Matthew's fruits. The tree was replaced, not abandoned, and the replacement came from the one other New Testament passage that argues from a source's inability to produce against its own nature. James 3:10's complaint — 'Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing' — is also the complaint Mormon's chapter is making about men whose works and intent disagree.

links.note: “A bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water.” The KJV's one occurrence of 'cannot bring forth', carrying James's fountain instead of Matthew's tree, with Matthew's 'neither can' clause reproduced under it. Neither source alone accounts for the sentence and both are needed, which is the mark of a composite rather than a recollection. That James's other chapter supplies 7:12-13's argument about the origin of good and evil gifts is a further reason to think James 3 is genuinely open in front of this discourse rather than remembered.
links.text: Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?

provenance.route: Matthew 6:24 (or Luke 16:13) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “two masters” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13, which are the same saying. Neither noun of Mormon's pair — servant, devil — is distinctive, and no clause is reproduced.
provenance.significance: What is borrowed is a shape: the impossibility of divided allegiance stated as a matched pair of exclusions. Matthew has 'either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other'; Mormon has 'a man being the servant of the Devil, cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ, he cannot be a servant of the Devil.' Luke's version supplies the noun — 'No servant can serve two masters' — where Matthew has 'no man', which is the only reason the mediation is left uncertain rather than assigned.

links.note: “A man being the servant of the Devil, cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ, he cannot be a servant of the Devil.” Held at moderate and typed as an echo: the figure of the two irreconcilable masters is unmistakable and no wording carries it. Recorded rather than passed over because the second half of 7:11 changes subject entirely from the first half — the fountain has nothing to do with service — and the reason it can is that a second and equally familiar saying has taken over the sentence.
links.text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, all things which are good, cometh of God; and that which is evil, cometh of the Devil: for the Devil is an enemy unto God, and fighteth against him continually, and inviteth and enticeth to sin, and to do that which is evil continually.

provenance.other: “every good gift” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “enticed” occurs in exactly three, and only James 1:14 uses it of temptation; the other two are Job 31:27 and Jeremiah 20:10.
provenance.significance: Moroni 7:12-13 is James 1:13-17 taken apart and reassembled as a pair of antitheses. James denies that God tempts ('Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God'), locates enticement in the man's own lust, and then asserts the positive: every good gift is from above, from the Father, with whom is no variableness. Mormon keeps James's two verbs of temptation and enticement but reassigns them — the devil 'inviteth and enticeth to sin', God's part 'inviteth and enticeth to do good' — so that James's asymmetry, in which God simply does not tempt, becomes a symmetry in which both sides solicit. The gain is a usable test, which is what the chapter is for; the loss is James's whole point that the impulse to evil is the man's own. What survives intact is the axiom: all good comes from one source. Mormon restates it at 7:24 with Christ in the place of God.

links.note: “All things which are good, cometh of God; and that which is evil, cometh of the Devil: for the Devil is an enemy unto God, and fighteth against him continually, and inviteth and enticeth to sin.” James 1:17's singleton supplies the axiom and James 1:14's rare verb supplies the mechanism, and both are in James's first chapter within four verses of each other. The machine ranked 1 John 3:8 here on the six-word run 'devil for the devil'; that is the article and the noun repeating across a clause boundary, and the excluded row explains why James rather than John accounts for the sentence.
links.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

provenance.other: No phrase is shared. What is shared is a three-part sequence: a tree known by its fruit (12:33), the impossibility of evil men speaking good (12:34, one of the three KJV verses with “being evil”), and the good and evil man each bringing forth out of his own treasure (12:35).
provenance.significance: Matthew 12:33-35 is the Synoptic passage that runs the whole of Mormon's argument in three verses, in his order: fruit test, evil men cannot produce good, good and evil each have their own source. Moroni 7:5-12 runs the same three in the same order across eight verses. The reason to record it as an echo rather than to build a link on it is that every individual borrowing in those eight verses can be traced to a better-worded source — 7:5 to Matthew 7:20, 7:10 to Matthew 7:11, 7:11 to James 3 — and Matthew 12 is the passage where the three already stand together.

links.note: “All things which are good, cometh of God; and that which is evil, cometh of the Devil.” Matthew 12:35's antithesis with God and the devil substituted for the two treasuries. Held at moderate and typed as an echo because there is no verbal contact at all; recorded because a reader who knows Matthew 12 will see the whole shape of Moroni 7:5-12 there and should be told the catalogue saw it and where it decided the actual wording came from.
links.text: A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things.

pericopes.text: But behold, that which is of God, inviteth and enticeth to do good continually; wherefore, every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God.
Wherefore take heed, my beloved brethren, that ye do not judge that which is evil to be of God, or that which is good and of God, to be of the Devil.

For behold, my brethren, it is given unto you to judge, that ye may know good from evil; and the way to judge is as plain, that ye may know with a perfect knowledge, as the daylight is from the dark night.—

For behold, the spirit of Christ is given to every man, that they may know good from evil; wherefore I shew unto you the way to judge: for every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ; wherefore ye may know with a perfect knowledge, it is of God;

provenance.other: “the manifestation of the Spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “given to every man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and they are the same verse. “Spirit of Christ” occurs in exactly two, Romans 8:9 and 1 Peter 1:11.
provenance.significance: Mormon is describing a universal endowment of discernment, and the KJV verse he reaches for is the one that makes the endowment universal — 'the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal'. Four verses further down the same chapter, 1 Corinthians 12:10 names the gift in question outright as 'discerning of spirits', which is precisely the faculty Moroni 7:14-17 is teaching his hearers to exercise. So the chapter Moroni's grandson will quote at Moroni 10:8-14 for the catalogue of gifts is already open here, forty-eight verses earlier, being used for the one gift the sermon needs. And the Pauline unit that begins at 1 Corinthians 12 is the unit that ends at 1 Corinthians 13, which is where this sermon ends.

links.note: “The spirit of Christ is given to every man, that they may know good from evil.” Five words reproduced from a KJV singleton with one substitution: Paul's 'the Spirit' becomes 'the spirit of Christ', which is Romans 8:9's phrase and which the chapter needs because its test is whether a thing 'persuadeth to believe in Christ'. The 1830 'that they may know' was regularized to 'that he may know' in 1920, against the KJV's own 'every man … to profit withal'; the plural is Mormon's, not Paul's. Note that this is the same Corinthian unit the chapter will quote entire at 7:45.
links.text: But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.

pericopes.text: but whatsoever thing persuadeth men to do evil, and believe not in Christ, and deny him, and serve not God, then ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of the Devil, for after this manner doth the Devil work: for he persuadeth no man to do good, no not one; neither doth his angels; neither doth they which subject themselves unto him.

provenance.route: Psalm 14:3 / Psalm 53:3 → Romans 3:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the route is not decidable from the wording
provenance.other: “doeth good, no, not one” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Psalm 14:3, Psalm 53:3 and Romans 3:12 — and the KJV renders all three identically. Moroni 7:17 has 'no man to do good, no not one'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's one genuinely undecidable mediation and it is worth recording as such. Psalm 14:3 and its doublet Psalm 53:3 say that none does good; Romans 3:12 quotes them to prove that all are under sin. Mormon inverts the subject: it is not that no man does good but that the devil 'persuadeth no man to do good, no not one'. The clause that in the Psalter and in Romans indicts humanity is here transferred to the devil's record, so a verse about universal depravity becomes a verse about the perfect consistency of the tempter. Recovering either context makes the inversion do work — the reader who knows that this is what scripture says about men is being told it is true instead of the one who tempts them.

links.note: “For he persuadeth no man to do good, no not one; neither doth his angels.” Four words of a clause the KJV has three times, in identical English each time, so the OT-or-NT question cannot be settled here: mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence between Psalm 14:3 and Romans 3:12, and it is right to. Recorded as 'uncertain' rather than defaulted (CONVENTIONS §7). Held at moderate because the phrase is short and formulaic in its own right; what raises it above an echo is that the Book of Mormon reproduces the KJV's odd doubled negation, 'no, not one', which is a translator's mannerism rather than ordinary English.
links.text: They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one.

pericopes.text: And now my brethren, seeing that ye know the light by which ye may judge, which light is the light of Christ, see that ye do not judge wrongfully: for with that same judgement which ye judge, ye shall also be judged.

provenance.other: “with what judgment ye judge” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Lukan parallel, Luke 6:37-38, has no judgment clause at all — 'Judge not, and ye shall not be judged' followed by 'with the same measure that ye mete' — so the two candidates are separable and the Book of Mormon has Matthew's.
provenance.significance: The third of Mormon's three visits to Matthew 7 and the one that closes the section. Matthew 7:1-2 opens the chapter Mormon has been quoting from since 7:5, and he arrives at its opening last, having used its middle (7:11) and its end (7:20) first. What he adds is the light: 'seeing that ye know the light by which ye may judge, which light is the light of Christ, see that ye do not judge wrongfully.' Matthew's warning is against judging at all; Mormon's is against judging badly, having spent fifteen verses arguing that his hearers are equipped to judge well. The reciprocity clause is kept because it is the sanction that makes the equipment matter.

links.note: “With that same judgement which ye judge, ye shall also be judged.” The KJV's one occurrence of the clause, with 'that same' interposed — which is Luke 6:38's adjective, not Matthew's, and the only Lukan trace in a sentence that is otherwise Matthew's throughout. The Book of Mormon already contains Matthew 7:2 word for word, in Christ's mouth at 3 Nephi 14:2, so this is a Nephite preacher quoting a saying his own scripture records; the wording here is neither 3 Nephi's nor quite the KJV's, which is what a preacher quoting from memory produces and what a transcriber does not. The 1830's 'judgement' was respelled in 1920.
links.text: For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.

pericopes.text: Wherefore I beseech of you, brethren, that ye should search diligently in the light of Christ, that ye may know good from evil; and if ye will lay hold upon every good thing, and condemn it not, ye certainly will be a child of Christ.

provenance.other: “hold fast that which is good” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni's verb is 'lay hold upon', which is not Paul's, and 'lay hold' occurs in fourteen KJV verses, none of them with a good thing as its object.
provenance.significance: Paul's couplet is a discrimination followed by a retention — 'Prove all things; hold fast that which is good' — and Moroni 7:19 is the same couplet in the same order at the seam of the sermon: search diligently in the light of Christ (prove), then lay hold upon every good thing and condemn it not (hold fast). It is worth noting because the phrase 'every good thing' becomes the sermon's own from here to 7:28, occurring six times in ten verses, and this is where it enters.

links.note: “If ye will lay hold upon every good thing, and condemn it not, ye certainly will be a child of Christ.” Held at moderate because the verb is changed and only the object survives: what identifies Paul is the pairing of a testing clause with a retaining clause, not any run of words. Recorded because 7:19 is the hinge on which the discourse turns from judging to faith, and because the formula it coins here — 'lay hold upon every good thing' — is a Book of Mormon phrase found only in this chapter.
links.text: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

pericopes.text: And now, my brethren, how is it possible that ye can lay hold upon every good thing?
And now I come to that faith, of which I said I would speak; and I will tell you the way whereby ye may lay hold on every good thing.

For behold, God knowing all things, being from everlasting to everlasting, behold, he sent angels to minister unto the children of men, to make manifest concerning the coming of Christ; and in Christ there should come every good thing.

provenance.other: “from everlasting to everlasting” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all in the Psalter: Psalm 90:2, 103:17 and 106:48. Of the three, only Psalm 90:2 predicates the phrase of God's own being — 'even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God' — where 103:17 predicates it of his mercy and 106:48 uses it as a doxological formula. Moroni 7:22 has 'God … being from everlasting to everlasting', which is 90:2's predication.
provenance.significance: The clause is doing argumentative work rather than doxological work, which is what selects the Psalm. Mormon needs God's eternity as the premise of a claim about foreknowledge — 'God knowing all things, being from everlasting to everlasting, behold, he sent angels' — so that the ministry of angels before Christ's coming can be explained as a provision made by someone outside time. Psalm 90 is the one Psalm about the difference between God's duration and man's, which is exactly the difference the verse needs.

links.note: “For behold, God knowing all things, being from everlasting to everlasting, behold, he sent angels to minister unto the children of men.” Six words of a formula the KJV has three times, in the one instance that says what Mormon's sentence needs it to say. Held at moderate: a phrase this liturgical could reach a nineteenth-century sermon without any particular Psalm behind it, and the discrimination among the three rests on grammar rather than on wording.
links.text: Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

pericopes.text: And God also declared unto prophets, by his own mouth, that Christ should come.

And behold, there were diverse ways that he did manifest things unto the children of men, which were good; and all things which are good, cometh of Christ, otherwise men were fallen, and there could no good thing come unto them.

Wherefore, by the ministering of angels, and by every word which proceeded forth out of the mouth of God, men began to exercise faith in Christ; and thus by faith, they did lay hold upon every good thing: and thus it was until the coming of Christ.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 8:3 → Matthew 4:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “proceedeth out of the mouth of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:4. Deuteronomy 8:3, the verse Matthew is quoting, reads 'out of the mouth of the LORD'. Moroni 7:25 reads 'proceeded forth out of the mouth of God' — the New Testament's noun, in the New Testament's phrase, with the participle put into the past tense the sentence needs.
provenance.significance: The divine name is the whole of the evidence and it settles the case: the Book of Mormon has the Gospel's 'God' and not the Pentateuch's 'LORD'. What the mediation then buys is a reading. Deuteronomy 8:3 is about manna and the wilderness diet; Matthew 4:4 is Christ refusing to make bread, in a temptation narrative. Mormon's sentence is about how men had faith before Christ came — 'by the ministering of angels, and by every word which proceeded forth out of the mouth of God' — and Matthew 4:11 ends the temptation with angels coming and ministering unto him. So both of Mormon's two channels of pre-advent faith, angels and the word of God's mouth, stand seven verses apart in the one Gospel passage he has taken the phrase from.

links.note: “By the ministering of angels, and by every word which proceeded forth out of the mouth of God, men began to exercise faith in Christ.” mediation-check.py returns 'no decisive divergence' on this pair, and it is wrong to — its word-level alignment groups Deuteronomy's five-word tail 'the LORD doth man live' against Matthew's single 'God' and so never sees that the Book of Mormon has one of them. CONVENTIONS §7 and ADJUDICATING §4 both put single common words in the adjudicator's hands rather than the tool's, and the divine name is decisive by eye. This is the kind of case the mediation apparatus exists for: one word, and the route through the New Testament is established.
links.text: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.

pericopes.text: And after that he came, men also were saved by faith in his name; and by faith, they become the sons of God. And as suredly as Christ liveth, he spake these words unto our fathers, saying, Whatsoever thing ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is good, in faith believing that ye shall receive, behold, it shall be done unto you.

provenance.route: John 16:23 + Matthew 21:22 + John 15:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Three KJV singletons, fused in one sentence and in this order: “ask the Father in my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (John 16:23); “believing, ye shall receive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (Matthew 21:22); “and it shall be done unto you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (John 15:7).
provenance.significance: The sentence is presented as a quotation of Christ — 'as suredly as Christ liveth, he spake these words unto our fathers, saying' — and what follows is three separate dominical promises about prayer welded into one. Two of the three come from the Farewell Discourse, John 15 and 16, and the third from the Matthean fig-tree episode; the joins are invisible because the KJV's English for asking and receiving is uniform across them. The one clause that belongs to none of the three is the qualifier Mormon needs, 'which is good' — the whole chapter has been an argument about how to tell what is good, and the qualifier is what makes an unlimited promise safe to preach. So the interpolation, not the borrowing, is the theology.

links.note: “Whatsoever thing ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is good, in faith believing that ye shall receive, behold, it shall be done unto you.” Three KJV singletons in sequence with one interpolation, and no single source accounts for more than a third of the sentence. Catalogued as a quotation on the citation formula and on the completeness of the reproduction rather than on the length of any one run; no individual run reaches Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and the composite is what makes the case. 'Whatsoever ye shall ask' by itself stands in four KJV verses, and the discrimination among them is 'the Father', which is John 16:23's alone.
links.text: And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

provenance.other: “become the sons of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: John 1:12 conditions the sonship on receiving him and believing on his name; Mormon conditions it on faith in his name — 'men also were saved by faith in his name; and by faith, they become the sons of God' — which is the same condition with the Johannine 'received him' dropped. The phrase returns at 7:48, where it is 1 John 3:1-2's rather than the Gospel's, so the chapter uses both Johannine forms of the sonship promise, the Gospel's at the head of the faith section and the Epistle's at the very end of the sermon.

links.note: “And by faith, they become the sons of God.” The KJV's one occurrence of the clause, reproduced exactly. 'Sons of God' on its own stands in eleven KJV verses and is worthless as evidence; the verb 'become' is what identifies the source, and it identifies it uniquely.
links.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

pericopes.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, hath miracles ceased, because that Christ hath ascended into heaven, and hath set down on the right hand of God, to claim of the Father his rights of mercy which he hath upon the children of men:

provenance.other: “on the right hand of God” occurs in six KJV verses and cannot identify a source on its own; “subject unto him” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 15:28 and 1 Peter 3:22. What selects 1 Peter is that it is the only KJV verse holding the ascension, the session at the right hand, and the subjection of angels together — and Moroni 7:27 and 7:30 hold the same three, in the same order, three verses apart.
provenance.significance: The argument of 7:27-30 is that the ascension did not end the ministry of angels, and 1 Peter 3:22 is the one verse in the Bible that makes the ascension and the subjection of angels a single fact: 'Who is gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God; angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him.' Mormon takes the objection from the first half of the verse — Christ has ascended, therefore miracles have ceased — and the answer from the second: 'For behold, they are subject unto him, to minister according to the word of his command.' The suppressed correspondence is that the objection and its refutation come from the same sentence, and a reader who recovers it finds Mormon's rhetorical question already answered in his source.

links.note: “Because that Christ hath ascended into heaven, and hath set down on the right hand of God.” Taken alone this clause would be undecidable among six KJV verses, and Mark 16:19 ('he was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God') is the closest of them for the two verbs. What raises the row above that is 7:30, where 'they are subject unto him' picks up the second half of 1 Peter 3:22, and the angels of that clause are the angels Mormon is arguing about. The link is placed here, where the wording begins, with the second contact recorded in recurrenceRefs. The 1830's 'hath ascended' and 'hath set down' were both made 'have' or left in 1920's regularization of this chapter's auxiliaries.
links.text: Who is gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God; angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him.

pericopes.text: for he hath answered the ends of the law, and he claimeth all those that hath faith in him; and they that have faith in him, will cleave unto every good thing; wherefore he advocateth the cause of the children of men; and he dwelleth eternally in the heavens.—

provenance.other: “the end of the law” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni's phrase is 'the ends of the law', plural, and “ends of the law” occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is that Christ is the terminus of the law for righteousness to everyone that believes; Mormon's is that Christ 'hath answered the ends of the law', where 'ends' has slid from terminus toward purpose — the law's demands are met rather than abolished. It is a small movement and a consequential one, since Mormon's clause makes Christ the satisfier of a claim and Paul's makes him its endpoint. The plural is what carries the change and the plural is not in the KJV.

links.note: “For he hath answered the ends of the law, and he claimeth all those that hath faith in him.” Held at moderate and typed conceptual: the singular phrase is a KJV singleton and Mormon does not reproduce it, he pluralizes it, which is either a deliberate reworking or evidence that Romans 10:4 is being remembered rather than consulted. Either way the sentence that follows — Christ claiming those who believe — is Romans 10:4's own second half in different words. The 1830's 'all those that hath faith' was corrected to 'who have' in 1920.
links.text: For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.

provenance.other: “advocate” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 2:1, where it is 'an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous'. Moroni 7:28 turns the noun into a verb: 'he advocateth the cause of the children of men'.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible names Christ an advocate once, and the Book of Mormon is using that one word in its one biblical sense, forensically, of a party pleading before the Father. What Mormon adds is the courtroom's other half: 7:27 has Christ 'claim of the Father his rights of mercy', which is a plea entered, and 7:28 has him advocating a cause, which is the plea pursued. Recovering 1 John 2:1's context supplies the defendant — 'if any man sin, we have an advocate' — and so supplies the ground of the plea that Mormon's sentence leaves unstated. This is the second of three passages in Moroni 7 taken from 1 John; 7:48 will take the third and longest.

links.note: “Wherefore he advocateth the cause of the children of men; and he dwelleth eternally in the heavens.” One word, and the KJV uses it once. The verbing is the Book of Mormon's own — 'advocateth' is in no KJV verse — but the theological content of the word arrives with it, which is why this is an allusion and not merely shared vocabulary: nothing in ordinary English makes 'advocate' the natural word for what the ascended Christ does, and the KJV has already made it so.
links.text: My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous:

pericopes.text: And because that he hath done this, my beloved brethren, hath miracles ceased? Behold I say unto you, Nay; neither hath angels ceased to minister unto the children of men.

provenance.other: “ministering spirits” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the only KJV verse in which ministering is the defining function of angels rather than something they happen to do.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 1:14 closes an argument that angels are lesser than the Son by assigning them a permanent office — 'sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation' — and Moroni 7:29 uses precisely that permanence against the objection that the ascension ended their work: 'neither hath angels ceased to minister unto the children of men'. If ministering is what angels are for, the Son's exaltation cannot have retired them, and that inference is available only from Hebrews. The verb governs the whole section: angels sent 'to minister' at 7:22, ministering at 7:29, the office of their ministry at 7:31, and 'angels appear and minister unto men' at 7:37.

links.note: “Neither hath angels ceased to minister unto the children of men.” The identifying evidence is not a run of words but a function: the KJV assigns angels the office of ministering in exactly one verse, and the Book of Mormon's whole angelology in this chapter is built on that office. Moroni substitutes 'the children of men' for Hebrews' 'them who shall be heirs of salvation', which universalizes the ministry — an important change, since Mormon's point is that angels come to unbelievers too, by way of the 'chosen vessels' of 7:31.
links.text: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?

pericopes.text: For behold, they are subject unto him, to minister according to the word of his command, shewing themselves unto them of strong faith and a firm mind, in every form of godliness.

provenance.other: “form of godliness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the power thereof” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and they are the same verse — 2 Timothy 3:5, 'Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof'. Both are also Book of Mormon hapaxes in this shape: 'form of godliness' occurs in no other Book of Mormon verse, and Moroni 7:30 and 7:32 are two verses apart.
provenance.significance: Paul's verse is a single antithesis and Mormon takes it apart, keeping both halves and dropping the 'but'. 2 Timothy 3:5 is a description of apostates who have the appearance of religion without its power; Moroni 7:30 has angels 'shewing themselves … in every form of godliness' and 7:32 has the Holy Ghost given 'place in their hearts, according to the power thereof'. What Paul separates in order to condemn, Mormon distributes across two verses in order to affirm: the form is real because angels wear it, and the power is real because the Spirit exercises it. The polarity is reversed and the vocabulary is untouched — which is what makes the borrowing visible, since neither phrase is available anywhere else in the King James Bible.

links.note: “Shewing themselves unto them of strong faith and a firm mind, in every form of godliness.” Two KJV singletons from a single verse, split across Moroni 7:30 and 7:32, with the source's condemnation inverted into a commendation. The link is placed at 7:30 where the first phrase stands, with 7:32 in recurrenceRefs. The 1830 'shewing' preserves the KJV spelling and was modernized in 1920 (CONVENTIONS §8); the same verse of 2 Timothy is used in the ordinary polemical direction at 2 Nephi 28:5, which makes the reversal here a choice rather than a misremembering.
links.text: Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.

pericopes.text: And the office of their ministry is, to call men unto repentance, and to fulfil and to do the work of the covenants of the Father which he hath made unto the children of men, to prepare the way among the children of men, by declaring the word of Christ unto the chosen vessels of the Lord, that they may bear testimony of him;

provenance.other: “chosen vessel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Acts 9:15 is the Lord's answer to Ananias about Saul — 'he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel'. Moroni 7:31 gives the office of angels as 'declaring the word of Christ unto the chosen vessels of the Lord, that they may bear testimony of him'. Both halves come across: the vessel and the bearing. Recovering the context supplies the mechanism the verse is describing, since Acts 9 is the KJV's chief narrative of a man commissioned by a heavenly visitation and then sent to preach — which is exactly the two-stage arrangement of Moroni 7:31, angels to the chosen vessels, chosen vessels to everyone else.

links.note: “By declaring the word of Christ unto the chosen vessels of the Lord, that they may bear testimony of him.” A KJV singleton pluralized, with Acts's 'to bear my name' answered by 'bear testimony of him'. What makes the row worth having is that it identifies the missing step in Mormon's argument: he has claimed at 7:29 that angels have not ceased, and the obvious objection is that most people never see one. Verse 31 answers it by making angelic ministry indirect, and the KJV verse it reaches for is the one where a visitation produces a preacher.
links.text: But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:

pericopes.text: and by so doing, the Lord God prepareth the way that the residue of men may have faith in Christ, that the Holy Ghost may have place in their hearts, according to the power thereof: and after this manner bringeth to pass the Father the covenants which he hath made unto the children of men.

provenance.route: Amos 9:12 → Acts 15:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “residue of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Amos 9:12, the verse James is quoting at the council, reads 'that they may possess the remnant of Edom' in the KJV; mediation-check.py returns one decisive point — the Book of Mormon has Acts's 'residue', not Amos's 'remnant' — and the two texts have almost nothing else in common in English. The phrase is also a Book of Mormon hapax.
provenance.significance: This is the cleanest mediation in the chapter and the result is not merely formal. The KJV's Amos and the KJV's Acts diverge here because Acts follows a Greek text in which Edom has become adam, mankind, and the possessing has become seeking; so 'the residue of men' exists in English only because the New Testament read its Old Testament differently. When Moroni 7:32 says that God 'prepareth the way that the residue of men may have faith in Christ', it is standing on the Septuagintal side of a textual split. What it borrows with the phrase is the use James made of it: at the Jerusalem council the verse is the proof that people outside the covenant are included without becoming Jews, and Moroni 7:32's residue are those who never saw an angel and are reached through the chosen vessels of 7:31.

links.note: “The Lord God prepareth the way that the residue of men may have faith in Christ.” A KJV singleton reproduced entire, from the one Old Testament citation in the New Testament whose English wording has no counterpart in the English Old Testament. The machine ranked Acts 15:17 first for this verse and it is right for once; the interest is in what the count adds, which is that the alternative reading of the same prophecy was available in the same Bible and is not the one used.
links.text: That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called, saith the Lord, who doeth all these things.

pericopes.text: And Christ hath said, If ye will have faith in me, ye shall have power to do whatsoever thing is expedient in me.
And he hath said, Repent all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me and be baptized in my name, and have faith in me, that ye may be saved.

And now my beloved brethren, if this be the case that these things are true which I have spoken unto you, and God will shew unto you with power and great glory at the last day, that they are true; and if they are true, hath the day of miracles ceased?

or hath angels ceased to appear unto the children of men? or hath he withheld the power of the Holy Ghost from them? or will he, so long as time shall last, or the earth shall stand, or there shall be one man upon the face thereof to be saved?

Behold I say unto you Nay, for it is by faith that miracles are wrought; and it is by faith that angels appear and minister unto men; wherefore if these things have ceased, wo be unto the children of men, for it is because of unbelief, and all is vain:

provenance.other: “worketh miracles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the only KJV verse that asks by what agency miracles are worked and answers 'the hearing of faith'.
provenance.significance: Paul's rhetorical question is whether the Spirit and the miracles come by the works of the law or by the hearing of faith, and the expected answer is faith. Moroni 7:37 states the answer as a proposition — 'it is by faith that miracles are wrought; and it is by faith that angels appear and minister unto men' — and then draws the consequence Paul does not draw, that if the miracles have stopped it is the faith that has failed and not God. That consequence is the whole burden of 7:37-38, and it is available only if Paul's question has already been answered Paul's way.

links.note: “It is by faith that miracles are wrought.” The verb and its object are a KJV singleton and the causal claim is that verse's own; what is not reproduced is any clause, which is why this is held at moderate and typed as an echo. The row is worth writing because it names the premise on which 7:37-38's argument turns, and because it belongs to the same Pauline vein — faith against works — that produced 7:7's Romans 4.
links.text: He therefore that ministereth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles among you, doeth he it by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?

pericopes.text: for no man can be saved, according to the words of Christ, save they shall have faith in his name; wherefore, if these things have ceased, then has faith ceased also; and awful is the state of man: for they are as though there had been no redemption made.

But behold, my beloved brethren, I judge better things of you, for I judge that ye have faith in Christ, because of your meekness: for if ye have not faith in him, then ye are not fit to be numbered among the people of his church.

provenance.other: “better things of you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 'But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation, though we thus speak.'
provenance.significance: The borrowing carries its rhetorical position with it, and that is the finding. Hebrews 6:9 is the turn after the severest warning in the epistle — the impossibility of renewing to repentance those who fall away — and its whole function is to tell the congregation that the warning was not about them. Moroni 7:37-38 has just delivered its own severest warning: 'wo be unto the children of men, for it is because of unbelief … awful is the state of man'. Then 7:39: 'But behold, my beloved brethren, I judge better things of you.' The adversative, the vocative 'beloved', the phrase itself, and the pastoral function are all four Hebrews'. A preacher who reached for these four words without Hebrews 6 in view would have had to reinvent the situation they were written for.

links.note: “But behold, my beloved brethren, I judge better things of you, for I judge that ye have faith in Christ, because of your meekness.” A KJV singleton with one verb changed — Hebrews' 'we are persuaded' becomes 'I judge', which is the chapter's own governing verb since 7:4's 'I judge these things of you' — reproduced at the exact rhetorical joint its source occupies. Ether 12 built extensively on Hebrews 6 and 11, so this is the same epistle re-entering the corpus in a different hand, three books later; ADJUDICATING §4 asks for the full link when the phrase crosses a book boundary, and the argument here is in any case its own.
links.text: But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation, though we thus speak.

pericopes.text: And again my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?

And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you, That ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal; and this because of your faith in him according to the promise;

provenance.other: “the power of his resurrection” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is a Book of Mormon hapax: Moroni 7:41 is the only verse in the book that contains it. “attain unto” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which Philippians 3:11 — 'if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead' — is the only one whose object is the resurrection.
provenance.significance: Two consecutive Pauline verses supply two consecutive Book of Mormon verses, in order. Moroni 7:40 asks 'How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?'; 7:41 answers 'ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal'. Philippians 3:10 has the power of his resurrection and 3:11 has attaining unto the resurrection of the dead. Mormon has taken Paul's two phrases and swapped their objects — Paul attains the resurrection and knows its power, Mormon attains faith and hopes for the raising — but the pair, the order and the rare idiom are Philippians'. Recovering the context supplies the hope that Mormon's section is defining: Philippians 3:11's 'if by any means' is hope in Paul's own uncertain voice, which is the mood of a section whose thesis is that faith without hope is impossible.

links.note: “That ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal.” A KJV singleton reproduced exactly, in a verse whose neighbour has the rare verb of the source's neighbour. The machine ranked Philippians 3:10 here on the six-word run and this is a case where the n-gram stream found the right verse; what it could not see is 7:40, one verse earlier, which is where the case is actually made.
links.text: That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death;

pericopes.text: wherefore, if a man have faith, he must needs have hope: for without faith there cannot be any hope.
And again: Behold I say unto you, That he cannot have faith and hope, save he shall be meek, and lowly of heart:

provenance.other: “meek and lowly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, where it is Christ's self-description: 'learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:29 attaches the pair to a promise of rest — 'and ye shall find rest unto your souls' — and Moroni 7:3 opened this sermon with entering into the rest of the Lord. So the chapter's first verse and its penultimate section stand at the two ends of one KJV sentence, and the condition Mormon imposes at 7:43 (no faith and hope without meekness) is the condition Matthew's invitation already made. What Mormon adds is exclusivity: 'none is acceptable before God, save the meek and lowly of heart', which turns an invitation into a gate.

links.note: “He cannot have faith and hope, save he shall be meek, and lowly of heart.” The KJV's one occurrence of the pair, and CONVENTIONS §8 applies with unusual clarity: the 1830 reads 'lowly of heart' at 7:43 and again at the first of 7:44's two occurrences, where the KJV reads 'lowly in heart', and the 1920 edition changed the second of them back to 'in' — that is, a later edition corrected the Book of Mormon toward its source, and did so inconsistently, leaving 'of' standing at 7:43. The direction of the change is the evidence. Alma 37:33-34 uses the same phrase, so this is the corpus's second author to reach for it.
links.text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

pericopes.text: if so, his faith and hope is vain, for none is acceptable before God, save the meek and lowly of heart; and if a man be meek and lowly in heart, and confesses by the power of the Holy Ghost, that Jesus is the Christ, he must needs have charity: for if he have not charity, he is nothing; wherefore he must needs have charity.

provenance.other: “but by the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:3, and it is the KJV's one statement that a true confession of Jesus is possible only by the Spirit. The predicate, however, is not Paul's: Paul has 'that Jesus is the Lord', and “that Jesus is the Christ” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — John 20:31, 1 John 2:22 and 1 John 5:1 — all Johannine. Moroni 7:44 has Paul's agency clause with John's predicate, and the machine ranked 1 John 2:22 here for exactly that reason.
provenance.significance: This is the door of the Pauline unit, and the sermon walks through it one verse before it reaches the hymn. 1 Corinthians 12:3 opens the discussion of gifts that runs to 12:31's 'more excellent way' and then into chapter 13; Moroni 7:44 states its confession-test and 7:45 quotes 13:4-7. The catalogue found the same manoeuvre at Ether 12:11, which entered the unit by 12:31, and at Moroni 7:16, which took 12:7. Three separate entrances into one Pauline chapter, by three different verses, and each time the exit is charity. The Johannine predicate matters too: what the Holy Ghost testifies is not Paul's lordship but John's messiahship, so the confession-test arrives already fused with the Epistle that will end the chapter at 7:48.

links.note: “If a man be meek and lowly in heart, and confesses by the power of the Holy Ghost, that Jesus is the Christ, he must needs have charity.” Paul's structure with John's predicate — the Spirit as the only agent of a true confession, and the confession itself in the Johannine form. Held at high rather than certain because no clause is reproduced intact: the case rests on the conjunction of Paul's mechanism with John's content in one sentence, and on the fact that the next verse quotes Paul's own chapter.
links.text: Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “have not charity” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 13:1, 13:2 and 13:3, which are the three limbs of one refrain. 13:2 is the limb whose apodosis is 'I am nothing', and Moroni has 'he is nothing'; 13:1's is 'sounding brass' and 13:3's is 'it profiteth me nothing', which the chapter has already used at 7:6.
provenance.significance: Mormon takes Paul's refrain apart and uses its three limbs at three different points of his sermon. 13:3's 'profiteth nothing' opened the discourse at 7:6, thirty-eight verses before charity was named; 13:2's 'I am nothing' arrives here as the hinge into the charity section; and 7:46 will restate 13:2 in the second person before quoting 13:8. The apodosis is the same each time in Paul and the protasis differs; in Mormon the apodosis is what recurs, and it recurs at exactly the joints of his argument.

links.note: “For if he have not charity, he is nothing; wherefore he must needs have charity.” Six words of Paul's refrain with the person changed, which is the change the third-person sermon requires and the only change made. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as a quotation because the clause is complete and the source is not in doubt: the next verse quotes four consecutive verses of the same chapter.
links.text: And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.

pericopes.text: And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things;

provenance.other: Every predicate in the verse is a KJV singleton or nearly so: “suffereth long” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, “and is kind” in exactly one, “seeketh not her own” in exactly one, “is not easily provoked” in exactly one, “thinketh no evil” in exactly one, “endureth all things” in exactly one. All six are 1 Corinthians 13:4-7, and they arrive here in the source's order.
provenance.significance: The two omissions are the finding. Moroni 7:45 reproduces 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 continuously and drops exactly two clauses: 'charity vaunteth not itself' from 13:4 and 'doth not behave itself unseemly' from 13:5 — “vaunteth not itself” and “behave itself unseemly” each occurring in exactly one KJV verse, so neither can have been lost in a paraphrase of some other text. What the two have in common is that both are about self-display before other people, and they are the only two clauses in Paul's list that are. Everything retained is either an inward disposition or an endurance. So the excision moves Paul's portrait of charity a step inward, which is the direction the whole sermon has been travelling since 7:6 replaced Paul's charity with 'real intent'. The other change is grammatical and equally consistent: Paul's asyndeton becomes a chain of 'and's, and Paul's three fresh subjects ('charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself') collapse into one, so that the verse reads as a single sentence about a single thing rather than as a list.

links.note: “And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.” Fifty-two words reproduced from four consecutive KJV verses with two clauses omitted and conjunctions added — comfortably above Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold, and the longest continuous biblical quotation in the book of Moroni. The machine ranked all four source verses in the top four for this verse, which almost never happens and is what a genuine block quotation looks like from the n-gram stream. Hardy's apparatus cross-references 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 here.
links.text: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,

pericopes.text: wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail;

provenance.other: “charity never faileth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “the greatest of these” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:13, which Moroni turns into 'the greatest of all'. 'All things must fail' answers 13:8's 'they shall fail … they shall cease … it shall vanish away'.
provenance.significance: This is the verse that explains the shape of the whole chapter, and it is the catalogue's principal claim about Moroni 7. 1 Corinthians 13:8 reads: 'Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.' Moroni 7:27-38 is a sustained interrogation of that half-verse — 'hath miracles ceased?' at 7:27, 'hath miracles ceased? … neither hath angels ceased to minister' at 7:29, 'hath the day of miracles ceased?' at 7:35, 'or hath angels ceased to appear?' at 7:36, 'if these things have ceased, wo be unto the children of men' at 7:37 — twelve verses arguing that the charismata have not ceased, ending at 7:46 by quoting the verse that said they would. Mormon's resolution is Paul's own: the gifts are not yet gone, but they are the kind of thing that goes, 'for all things must fail', and the one that does not is charity. Read this way the sermon is not two sermons — a defence of miracles and a hymn to charity — but one argument, and 1 Corinthians 13:8 is the hinge nobody sees until verse 46. Neither text says this; the arrangement says it.

links.note: “If ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail.” Three separate contacts with 1 Corinthians 13 in one verse: 13:2's refrain in the second person, 13:8's KJV-singleton opening reproduced word for word, and 13:13's superlative with 'all' for 'these'. What makes the row more than an inventory is that 13:8's second half has been the chapter's subject since verse 27, which is argued in the significance field. Hardy's apparatus cross-references 1 Corinthians 13:2-8 here, a range that covers the composite exactly.
links.text: Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.

pericopes.text: but charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with them.

provenance.route: Ecclesiastes 8:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon (1830); the 1920 edition's reading points instead at Isaiah 3:10
provenance.other: “it shall be well with them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 8:12, 'surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God'. “it shall be well with him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 3:10, 'Say ye to the righteous, that it shall be well with him'. The 1830 has the first; the 1920 emended to the second.
provenance.significance: The interest of this row is entirely editorial and it is a clean instance of CONVENTIONS §8. The 1830 reads 'whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with them', which reproduces Ecclesiastes 8:12's clause exactly; the 1920 changed 'them' to 'him' to agree with the singular 'whoso', and in doing so moved the clause off one KJV singleton and onto another. Whichever verse stood behind the sentence, the modern text cannot be used to decide, and a reader working from it would find Isaiah where the first edition has Qoheleth. Ecclesiastes 8:12 is also the better fit for the sense: its subject is a verdict deferred to the end, reached in spite of appearances, which is Mormon's 'at the last day'.

links.note: “Whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with them.” Held at moderate: the clause is a common English idiom and its appearance in the 1830 in exactly the KJV's plural form may be grammatical accident rather than borrowing. The row is written because the 1830 and 1920 readings are each a KJV singleton and each a different one, which makes this the chapter's clearest demonstration that the running text choice is evidence and not housekeeping.
