links.whyNot: 'It shall be well with' occurs in seven KJV verses and the idiom was ordinary in nineteenth-century devotional English; a reader who takes the agreement with Ecclesiastes 8:12 as an artifact of the plural 'whoso' construction, and not as a quotation, has made a defensible judgment. Nothing else of Ecclesiastes 8 is present in the chapter.
links.text: Though a sinner do evil an hundred times, and his days be prolonged, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, which fear before him:

pericopes.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son Jesus Christ, that ye may become the sons of God, that when he shall appear, we shall be like him: for we shall see him as he is, that we may have this hope, that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.

provenance.other: “shall be like him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “we shall see him as he is” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both 1 John 3:2; the eighteen-word run 'that when he shall appear, we shall be like him: for we shall see him as he is' is reproduced without a variant. “hath bestowed” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, of which 1 John 3:1 is the one whose object is love; “this hope” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “as he is pure” occurs in exactly one, both 1 John 3:3.
provenance.significance: Moroni runs 1 John 3:1, 3:2 and 3:3 in order and reverses the logic of the third. John's sequence is: the Father has bestowed love, we are called the sons of God (3:1); when he appears we shall be like him (3:2); and every man that hath this hope purifieth himself (3:3) — hope produces purity. Mormon's sentence inverts the last step into a petition: pray to be filled with this love, that ye may become the sons of God, that we may be like him, 'that we may have this hope, that we may be purified even as he is pure'. Hope is no longer the possession that makes a man purify himself but a thing prayed for, downstream of the love. That is the chapter's own doctrine imposed on its source — 7:40-42 has already argued that hope is what faith becomes and that charity is what hope requires — and it is the last thing the sermon does. It also completes an arc: 7:1 announced faith, hope and charity out of 1 Corinthians 13:13, and 7:48 ends with love, sonship and hope out of 1 John 3, so the two great New Testament passages on love frame the discourse at both ends.

links.note: “Pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son Jesus Christ, that ye may become the sons of God, that when he shall appear, we shall be like him: for we shall see him as he is, that we may have this hope, that we may be purified even as he is pure.” An eighteen-word run of 1 John 3:2 reproduced without variation — above Skousen's threshold — inside a frame built from 3:1 and 3:3, and the whole in the source's order. The pronoun shift from 'ye' to 'we' in mid-sentence is the KJV's own at that point and is one more mark of transcription rather than recollection. 'With all the energy of heart' is in no KJV verse; 'energy' occurs nowhere in the King James Bible, which makes the one phrase Mormon adds the one phrase that could not have come from his source. Hardy's apparatus cross-references 1 John 3:2-3 at this verse.
links.text: Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.

pericopes.text: An epistle of my father Mormon, written to me, Moroni; and it was written unto me soon after my calling to the ministry. And on this wise did he write unto me, saying:
My beloved son Moroni, I rejoice exceedingly that your Lord Jesus Christ hath been mindful of you, and hath called you to his ministry, and to his holy work.

links.text: To Timothy, my dearly beloved son: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

provenance.other: “my dearly beloved son” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 1:2, where it addresses a young minister; “my beloved son” in that sense occurs in one other, 1 Corinthians 4:17, of Timotheus again. Every other KJV occurrence of “my beloved Son” is the voice from heaven at the baptism or the transfiguration.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 4:17, which drops the intensifier and is therefore verbally nearer, but stands in a letter to a congregation rather than to the son.
provenance.significance: The KJV gives exactly one model for a letter from an old minister to a young one he calls his son, and Moroni 8 takes the whole of it: the address (8:2), the constant remembrance in prayer (8:3, and 2 Timothy 1:3), the charge to a ministry lately received (8:2, and 2 Timothy 1:6), and a closing that hopes for a meeting the writer does not expect to get (8:27-30, and 2 Timothy 4:6-9). Mormon is writing 2 Timothy, and like 2 Timothy it is the letter of a man who says plainly that he may not survive to write another.

links.note: “My beloved son Moroni, I rejoice exceedingly that your Lord Jesus Christ hath been mindful of you, and hath called you to his ministry, and to his holy work.” The address is the Pastoral Epistles' and not the Gospels': in the KJV a father calls a minister 'my beloved son' only at 2 Timothy 1:2 and 1 Corinthians 4:17, and both times the son is Timothy. What follows in Moroni 8:2 is the same clause 2 Timothy 1:6 supplies — a gift or calling to ministry that the older man is writing to stir up. Catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation because the shared run is three words; the case rests on the address plus the situation plus the prayer clause at 8:3, not on any one of them.

pericopes.text: I am mindful of you always in my prayers, continually praying unto God the Father, in the name of his holy child, Jesus, that he, through his infinite goodness and grace, will keep you through the endurance of faith on his name to the end.

links.text: For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers;

provenance.other: “always in my prayers” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 1:9 and Philemon 1:4; “in my prayers” in exactly four, adding Ephesians 1:16 and 2 Timothy 1:3. All four are Pauline letter-openings and all four attach the phrase to a verb of ceaseless remembrance — 'without ceasing' at Romans 1:9 and 2 Timothy 1:3, 'cease not' at Ephesians 1:16.
provenance.significance: Moroni 8:3 keeps both halves of the formula and redistributes them: Romans' 'without ceasing' becomes 'continually praying', and 'mindful' — which is 2 Timothy 1:4's word, in the same opening — replaces 'make mention'. The result is a sentence assembled out of the four KJV verses that share the phrase rather than copied from any one of them, which is what makes the formula, and not a verse, the unit being borrowed.

links.note: “I am mindful of you always in my prayers, continually praying unto God the Father, in the name of his holy child, Jesus.” Two of the KJV's four 'in my prayers' verses read 'always in my prayers', and Romans 1:9 is the one with 'of you' rather than 'of thee' — which matters less than it looks, since Mormon's 'you' is a single addressee. The tell that this is the Pastoral formula and not Romans alone is 'mindful': it is 2 Timothy 1:4's verb, four words after 2 Timothy 1:3's 'in my prayers', and it is not in Romans 1:9 at all. 'His holy child, Jesus' is Acts 4:27 and 4:30, the only KJV verses that call Jesus God's 'holy child', and it is worth noting that both stand in a prayer.

links.text: And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.

provenance.other: “endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:22 (Matthew 24:13 reads 'endure unto the end', Mark 13:13 'shall endure unto the end').
provenance.significance: Matthew 10:22's promise is made to men who are about to be hated and killed for the name; Mormon writes it to a son he expects not to see again, in a chapter that ends by predicting the destruction of their nation. The clause is the Book of Mormon's most-repeated borrowing, and here it returns to something like Matthew's original setting.

links.note: “Will keep you through the endurance of faith on his name to the end.” The formula is adjudicated at 1 Nephi 22:31 and used across the corpus; the reason for a row here rather than a cross-reference is that Mormon has nominalized it — 'the endurance of faith', a noun the KJV never forms — and has kept 'on his name', which is Matthew 10:22's 'for my name's sake' turned into the object of the enduring rather than its cause. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is by this point the corpus's own idiom as much as the KJV's.
links.whyNot: By Moroni the clause has been used so often in the Book of Mormon that a fresh borrowing from Matthew cannot be shown; a reader may fairly regard this as the corpus quoting itself.

pericopes.text: And now my son, I speak unto you concerning that which grieveth me exceedingly: for it grieveth me that there should disputations rise among you.
For if I have learned the truth: there has been disputations among you concerning the baptism of your little children.

links.text: When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.

provenance.other: “disputation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 15:2, and “no small dissension” in the same one. Acts 15:24's “troubled you with words” and “certain which went out from us” are likewise KJV singletons.
provenance.significance: Acts 15 is the KJV's one account of a dispute over whether a rite must be administered, referred to the church's leadership, and settled by a letter sent to the congregation that was troubled. Moroni 8 is that letter again with the rite changed: 'the baptism of your little children' for 'Ye must be circumcised'. The reader who recovers Acts 15 finds Mormon's own ruling waiting at 8:8 — 'the law of circumcision is done away in me' — which is the decision the Jerusalem letter reached, quoted as the ground of a decision about baptism. The chapter argues from the precedent while sounding as though it were only reasoning.

links.note: “There has been disputations among you concerning the baptism of your little children.” The KJV uses 'disputation' once, at Acts 15:2, of the quarrel over circumcision; the 1830 uses 'disputations' twice in two verses (8:4, 8:5) for a quarrel over infant baptism, and then names circumcision outright at 8:8. The verbal contact is one rare word, but the form of the whole chapter follows Acts 15: a rite disputed in a distant congregation (15:1-2), the matter referred upward (Moroni 8:7, 'I inquired of the Lord concerning the matter'), and the answer sent back as a letter that says what the troublers were saying and denies it. Catalogued at 8:5 rather than 8:4 because this is the verse that joins the rare word to the disputed rite. 1830's 'has been disputations' was corrected to 'have' in 1920.

pericopes.text: And now my son, I desire that ye should labor diligently, that this gross error should be removed from among you: for, for this intent I have written this epistle.
For immediately after I had learned these things of you, I inquired of the Lord concerning the matter. And the word of the Lord came to me by the power of the Holy Ghost, saying,

Listen to the words of Christ, your Redeemer, your Lord and your God. Behold, I came into the world not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance; the whole need no physician, but they that are sick; wherefore little children are whole, for they are not capable of committing sin; wherefore the curse of Adam is taken from them in me, that it hath no power over them: and the law of circumcision is done away in me.

links.text: And Jesus answering said unto them, They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick.

provenance.other: “whole need not a physician” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 9:12 and Luke 5:31; “not to call the righteous” in exactly two, Mark 2:17 and Luke 5:32; “sinners to repentance” in three. Luke is the only book where the two clauses that Moroni 8:8 reproduces both stand in their Moroni form, and “came into the world” is a KJV singleton at 1 Timothy 1:15, “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners”.
provenance.alternative: Mark 2:17, which Hardy's apparatus cross-references alongside Matthew and Luke, and which holds both clauses in one verse — but reads 'have no need of the physician', which Moroni does not have.
provenance.significance: The mediation test is unusually clean and it decides against two thirds of Hardy's row. Matthew 9:13 reads 'I am not come to call'; Moroni reads 'I came…not to call', which is Mark's and Luke's. Mark 2:17 reads 'they that are whole have no need of the physician'; Moroni reads 'the whole need no physician', which keeps Matthew's and Luke's verb-first shape. Luke 5:31-32 is the only place in the KJV where both of Moroni's forms stand together. What Moroni adds is the expansion 'I came into the world', and the KJV's one verse joining that phrase to sinners is 1 Timothy 1:15 — so the saying arrives with a Pauline gloss attached. Then comes the inference the Gospels never draw: if the physician is for the sick, and little children are whole, the sacrament of the sick does not apply to them. Christ's defence of eating with sinners is turned into an argument for withholding a rite.

links.note: “I came into the world not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance; the whole need no physician, but they that are sick.” The chapter's central borrowing and its argumentative hinge. Two clauses of the synoptic pericope are reproduced nearly verbatim, and their order is reversed: in all three Gospels the physician comes first and the calling second, in Moroni the calling comes first and the physician second, because the word Mormon needs to pick up is 'whole', which then governs the rest of the verse ('wherefore little children are whole'). The reversal is the argument. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 9:12-13, Mark 2:17 and Luke 5:31-32 here; the wording is Luke's, and the note above says on what evidence. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold as a single run and catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the two reproduced clauses and the rarity of both.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Moro 8.8 (Matthew 9:12-13, Mark 2:17, Luke 5:31-32)

links.text: But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ.

provenance.other: “is done away in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:14, where the full phrase is “done away in Christ”. Moroni 8:8 has “done away in me” in the mouth of Christ, which is the same phrase with the pronoun that the speaker requires.
provenance.significance: Recovering 2 Corinthians 3 makes the substitution work harder than it looks. What is 'done away in Christ' there is the vail on the reading of the old testament, and the chapter's argument is that a glory belonging to the ministration of death is abolished by a ministration of the spirit. Moroni 8 applies the formula to a specific old-testament ordinance, circumcision, and then — this is the point — uses the abolition of the sign given to infants as the reason for withholding a sign from infants. Paul's vail becomes Mormon's knife.

links.note: “And the law of circumcision is done away in me.” The KJV forms 'is done away in' once, and there it is 'done away in Christ'; here Christ is speaking, so the phrase is unchanged except for the pronoun it must take. The link matters beyond its four words because it supplies the legal warrant the chapter needs: circumcision is the rite the Bible does administer to those who cannot consent, and the whole force of 8:8 is that the one such rite has been abolished by the same speaker who is now refusing another. Note that Ether 4:15 uses the same 2 Corinthians 3 material for the vail itself, which is the source's own subject; Moroni 8:8 takes the formula and leaves the vail.

links.text: Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come.

provenance.other: Romans 5:14 is the KJV's one verse describing people over whom Adam's consequence reigns although they 'had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression'. No distinctive phrase is shared; the contact is the proposition.
provenance.significance: Romans 5:12-14 is the passage on which the western case for infant baptism was actually built — death passing upon all men, reigning even over those who have not themselves sinned. Moroni 8:8 states the same anthropology and reverses its consequence: the curse of Adam is real, it is precisely what the incapable inherit, and it is taken away from them in Christ without a rite. The chapter is not ignoring the proof text; it is answering it.

links.note: “Wherefore the curse of Adam is taken from them in me, that it hath no power over them.” Almost no shared wording, and the row is here because the doctrine is exactly Romans 5:12-14's and exactly inverted. Paul's argument runs Adam → death over the non-transgressing → the need of the second Adam; Mormon's runs Adam → curse over the non-transgressing → already removed in the second Adam, therefore no baptism. Catalogued as an allusion rather than an echo because 'the curse of Adam' has no other biblical locus that states the case, and moderate rather than high because the wording will not carry the claim on its own.
links.whyNot: There is no distinctive verbal contact. A reader who requires shared phrasing should decline this row and read 8:8's Adam clause as the Book of Mormon's own doctrine, stated in 2 Nephi 2 long before this chapter.

pericopes.text: And after this manner did the Holy Ghost manifest the word of God unto me; wherefore my beloved son, I know that it is solemn mockery before God, that ye should baptize little children.

links.text: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.

provenance.other: “God is not mocked” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's twenty-one other occurrences of 'mocked' are all of one person mocking another; Galatians 6:7 is the only one whose object is God.
provenance.significance: Galatians 6:7's mockery is self-deception about consequences — 'be not deceived… whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap'. Moroni's is a rite performed as though God could be induced to count it. Both make the charge against religious practice rather than against blasphemy, and both stand in letters whose subject is a rite wrongly required.

links.note: “It is solemn mockery before God, that ye should baptize little children.” 'Mockery' is not a KJV word at all, and the one KJV verse that makes God the object of mocking is Galatians 6:7 — in the letter that is also behind 8:24's 'under the curse of a broken law'. Mormon uses the charge twice, here and at 8:23, and both times of a sacramental act rather than of scorn. Recorded as an echo because the shared element is a single idea and a single root; the argument for it is that Galatians is demonstrably in view elsewhere in the same chapter.

pericopes.text: Behold I say unto you, that this thing shall ye teach, repentance and baptism unto they which are accountable and capable of committing sin; yea, teach parents that they must repent and be baptized, and humble themselves as their little children, and they shall all be saved with their little children;

links.text: Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.other: “humble himself as” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 18:4 ('Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child'); “become as little children” in exactly one, Matthew 18:3. Both are in the same speech, and Moroni 8:10 has both moves in one clause.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:2-4 is the passage a defender of infant baptism has least use for and Mormon has most. Christ sets a child in the midst as the pattern for adults; the child is the standard, not the candidate. Moroni 8:10 draws the conclusion the Gospel leaves implicit — if children are the model of the state baptism aims at, then baptism is for those who are not yet in it — and turns the parents into the ones who must be converted. That the same evangelist's 19:14 says 'of such is the kingdom of heaven' completes the case: the children are already inside.

links.note: “Teach parents that they must repent and be baptized, and humble themselves as their little children, and they shall all be saved with their little children.” The KJV's one 'humble himself as' verse is about a little child, and the verse before it is the KJV's one 'become as little children'. Mormon combines them and adds the plural possessive: not 'as this little child' but 'as their little children', which makes the child in the midst the reader's own. Note what the sentence does to Matthew's order of salvation — in Matthew the child-likeness is the condition of entering the kingdom, here it is a thing parents are taught alongside repentance and baptism, and the children are saved 'with' them rather than through them.

links.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “for the remission of sins” occurs in exactly five KJV verses; “repent and be baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:38, which also carries the gift of the Holy Ghost that Moroni 8:26 reaches at the end of its chain.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:38-39 is the other classical proof text for infant baptism — 'the promise is unto you, and to your children' — and Moroni 8:10-11 quotes the command and stops one verse short of the promise. Whether or not that is deliberate, the effect is that the chapter's positive statement of the ordinance is drawn from the verse most often used against its conclusion.

links.note: “Repentance and baptism unto they which are accountable… teach parents that they must repent and be baptized.” The order repent-then-be-baptized-unto-remission is Acts 2:38's, and 8:11's 'unto the remission of sins' completes it. Moderate rather than high: the chain is the Book of Mormon's standing formula by this point in the corpus (2 Nephi 31, 3 Nephi 30, Mormon 7), so this is Mormon using an idiom he has inherited as much as reaching for Acts. The row is worth having anyway because the argument of the chapter turns on who the imperative can be addressed to, which is the one thing Acts 2:38 makes explicit and Mormon exploits: only the accountable can be commanded to repent. 1830 reads 'unto they which are accountable', corrected to 'those who' in 1920.
links.whyNot: The repent-and-be-baptized formula is corpus-wide and cannot be shown to be a fresh borrowing here rather than the Book of Mormon's own catechetical language.

pericopes.text: and their little children need no repentance, neither baptism. Behold, baptism is unto repentance to the fulfilling the commandments unto the remission of sins.

But little children are alive in Christ, even from the foundation of the world: if not so, God is a partial God, and also a changeble God, and a respecter to persons: for how many little children have died without baptism.

links.text: For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.

provenance.other: “in Adam all die” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “shall all be made alive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are 1 Corinthians 15:22. “alive in Christ” as such occurs in no KJV verse; the nearest is Romans 6:11, 'alive unto God through Jesus Christ'.
provenance.significance: The chapter's slogan — 'little children are alive in Christ' — is 1 Corinthians 15:22's second clause compressed into an adjective phrase, and 8:8's 'the curse of Adam is taken from them in me' is its first clause denied for one class of persons. So the two halves of Paul's antithesis are separated across four verses and one of them is cancelled. Recover the source and the argument reads: as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive — and for those incapable of sin the second clause has already happened.

links.note: “But little children are alive in Christ, even from the foundation of the world.” The phrase is not in the KJV, and the verse that supplies both of its terms is 1 Corinthians 15:22, the KJV's one home for 'in Adam all die' and 'in Christ shall all be made alive'. Read with 8:8's curse of Adam, the pair of borrowings is a single Pauline sentence taken apart and used on both sides of the chapter's argument. Mormon repeats the slogan at 8:19 and 8:22, where it is joined to Romans 8:1's 'no condemnation'. 'Even from the foundation of the world' is common KJV property (six verses) and does not identify a source of its own.

links.text: Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:

provenance.other: “respecter of persons” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 10:34, Peter's 'Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons'. The 1830 Moroni 8:12 reads 'a respecter to persons', with the preposition of James 2:9's 'ye have respect to persons'; 1920 corrected it to 'of'.
provenance.significance: Peter says it at the moment the rite of admission is opened to people the law had excluded, and says it immediately before ordering that those people be baptized (Acts 10:47-48). Moroni 8:12 uses the same sentence to argue that a class of persons must be excluded from the same rite — not because God prefers them less, but because a God who is no respecter of persons cannot have made salvation turn on whether a child lived long enough to be washed. The premise is Peter's; the conclusion runs the other way.

links.note: “If not so, God is a partial God, and also a changeble God, and a respecter to persons: for how many little children have died without baptism.” The KJV's one 'respecter of persons' verse, negated by Peter and here made the reductio: infant baptism, if it saves, makes God what Acts 10:34 says he is not. The 1830's 'a respecter to persons' is worth noting under CONVENTIONS §8 — it is a fusion of Acts 10:34's noun with James 2:9's preposition, and 1920's correction to 'of' moved the text back toward the KJV. 1830's 'changeble' for 'changeable' is a spelling, not a variant reading. Mormon restates the whole clause at 8:18.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, if little children could not be saved without baptism, these must have gone to an endless hell.

Behold I say unto you, That he that supposeth that little children needeth baptism, is in the gall of bitterness, and in the bonds iniquity: for he hath neither faith, hope, nor charity; wherefore, should he be cut off while in the thought, he must go down to hell.

links.text: For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.

provenance.other: “gall of bitterness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “bond of iniquity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Acts 8:23. The 1830 reads “in the bonds iniquity”, dropping the preposition and pluralizing the noun; 1920 restored “bonds of iniquity”, which is nearer the KJV in the preposition and further from it in the number.
provenance.significance: Peter says this to Simon Magus, who has just tried to buy the power of conferring the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands — that is, to a man whose sin is a false relation to a sacrament of initiation. Moroni 8:14 puts the same words on a man who administers a sacrament of initiation to those who cannot receive it. Both are charged with treating an ordinance as a thing that can be made to work by being performed. And the next verse of Acts is Peter's 'Repent therefore of this thy wickedness', which is what Moroni 8:16 goes on to demand — 'they shall perish, except they repent'.

links.note: “Is in the gall of bitterness, and in the bonds iniquity.” Eight words of a nine-word KJV verse, both of whose distinctive phrases are singletons; there is no other candidate. The chapter's rhetoric is now running on Acts's two confrontations with sorcerers — Peter and Simon here, Paul and Elymas at 8:16 — and the pairing is the finding: Mormon condemns the baptizers of infants in the two forms of words the KJV reserves for men who trade in the appearance of spiritual power. Note the 1830 reading: the missing 'of' makes 'bonds iniquity' a genitive by juxtaposition, which is the kind of error a text produces when it is reproducing a remembered phrase rather than copying it.

pericopes.text: For awful is the wickedness to suppose that God saveth one child because of baptism, and the other must perish because he hath no baptism.

Wo be unto him that shall pervert the ways of the Lord after this manner, for they shall perish, except they repent. Behold, I speak with boldness, having authority from God; and I fear not what man can do: for perfect love casteth out all fear;

links.text: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.

provenance.other: “perfect love casteth out” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni adds one word: “casteth out all fear”.
provenance.significance: 1 John 4:18 continues 'because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.' Moroni 8:16 has just said 'I fear not what man can do', and 8:21 will threaten those who pervert the ordinance with 'death, hell, and an endless torment'. So the torment 1 John attaches to the one who fears is transferred, in the space of five verses, to the one who is to be feared — the writer keeps the perfect love, and hands the torment to his opponents.

links.note: “For perfect love casteth out all fear.” A KJV singleton reproduced with one word added, and the addition is doing something: 1 John's 'fear' is fear of judgment, and Mormon's 'all fear' has to cover the fear of man he has just disclaimed in the same sentence. This is the hinge of the chapter's second half — 8:17's 'charity, which is everlasting love' and 'I love little children with a perfect love' both depend on it, as does the 'perfect love' of 8:26. The charity vocabulary itself is 1 Corinthians 13's and is adjudicated at Moroni 7:44-46.

links.text: In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me.

provenance.other: The psalm states its refrain twice: 56:4 'I will not fear what flesh can do unto me' and 56:11 'I will not be afraid what man can do unto me'. “what man can do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 56:11; “I will not fear what” belongs to 56:4 and to Hebrews 13:6. Moroni's “I fear not what man can do” has 56:4's verb and 56:11's noun, and nothing that is only Hebrews'.
provenance.alternative: Hebrews 13:6, 'we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me' — which pairs boldness with fearlessness of man exactly as Moroni 8:16 does, and which is quoting Psalm 118:6, not Psalm 56.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 13:6 supplies the sentence's shape and Psalm 56 supplies its words. That is a genuinely divided result and it is recorded as one: had the Book of Mormon taken this from Hebrews it would read 'what man shall do', and it does not; had it taken it from Psalm 56:4 alone it would read 'what flesh can do', and it does not. What it has is the psalm's twin refrain conflated — the verb of the first statement with the noun of the second — which is what a text does when it is quoting a psalm from memory rather than from a page.

links.note: “Behold, I speak with boldness, having authority from God; and I fear not what man can do.” `mediation-check.py` on Psalm 56:4 against Hebrews 13:6 returns one decisive point for the Psalm ('can', not 'shall') and none for Hebrews; run against Psalm 56:11 it returns one each way ('fear' with Hebrews, 'can' with the Psalm), and the resolution is that 'fear' is also Psalm 56:4's word. So both discriminating words are available inside Psalm 56 and neither is uniquely Hebrews', and the mediation is direct-OT. The countervailing evidence is contextual and is stated in `provenance.alternative`: only Hebrews 13:6 puts boldness of speech next to fearlessness of man, which is precisely Moroni's pairing here and again at 8:21 ('I speak it boldly'). 'Having authority' is a KJV singleton at Matthew 7:29, of Christ's manner of teaching against the scribes' — a fair description of what Mormon is claiming in this sentence.

links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.other: “pervert the right ways of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10. “pervert the” occurs in six, of which the other five pervert judgment, words, or the gospel — none of them the Lord's ways. Moroni 8:16 drops 'right' and keeps the rest.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:10 is Paul's rebuke of Elymas the sorcerer, and Moroni 8:14 has just used Peter's rebuke of Simon the sorcerer. The KJV contains exactly two scenes in which an apostle denounces a magician to his face, and Moroni 8 draws on both of them within three verses, in their canonical order, to condemn the baptizers of little children. Neither Acts passage is about baptism; what they share with Moroni 8 is a man who mishandles the machinery of the sacred and an apostle with the authority to say so out loud. That is also why 8:16's 'having authority from God' is in the sentence — the borrowing is not only of words but of a warrant to speak them.

links.note: “Wo be unto him that shall pervert the ways of the Lord after this manner, for they shall perish, except they repent.” A KJV singleton with one word dropped, and the drop is intelligible: Acts's 'right ways' contrasts with a crooked path, while Mormon's opponents are perverting the ways themselves. The row's real interest is its neighbour — see Moroni 8:14, where the words are Peter's to Simon Magus. Taken together the two verses are this catalogue's proposal that Mormon's model for denouncing a sacramental abuse is Acts's model for denouncing sorcery. Nothing in either Acts passage concerns children or baptism, and the machine proposed neither; the row is offered as an argument, not as an identification.

pericopes.text: and I am filled with charity, which is everlasting love; wherefore all children are alike unto me; wherefore I love little children with a perfect love; and they are all alike, and partakers of salvation.
For I know that God is not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity.
Little children cannot repent; wherefore it is awful wickedness to deny the pure mercies of God unto them, for they are all alive in him because of his mercy.
And he that saith that little children needeth baptism, denieth the mercies of Christ, and setteth at nought the atonement of him and the power of his redemption.

Wo unto such, for they are in danger of death, hell, and an endless torment. I speak it boldly, God hath commanded me. Listen unto them and give heed, or they stand against you at the judgement seat of Christ.

links.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10; “stand before the judgment seat” in exactly one, Romans 14:10 (2 Corinthians 5:10 reads 'appear before'). “set at nought” occurs in five, one of which is Romans 14:10.
provenance.significance: Romans 14 is Paul's ruling that believers must not condemn one another over a disputed observance — meats and days — because both parties will stand at the same judgment seat. Moroni 8:20-21 borrows the verse to do the opposite: it names one side of a disputed observance and tells them that the other side will stand against them there. The metalepsis is sharp. Recover Romans 14 and the sentence Mormon is using to condemn his opponents is the sentence Paul wrote to stop exactly that.

links.note: “Setteth at nought the atonement of him… or they stand against you at the judgement seat of Christ.” The two rare elements are split across 8:20 and 8:21 in Romans 14:10's own order — 'set at nought' first, 'stand before the judgment seat of Christ' second — and the KJV holds them together in one verse only here. The mediation between the two 'judgment seat of Christ' verses is decided by the verb: Moroni has 'stand', which is Romans 14:10's, not 2 Corinthians 5:10's 'appear'. Note the 1830 'judgement seat', modernized in 1920 to the hyphenated 'judgment-seat'. The phrase recurs across the corpus (2 Nephi 33:7, 3 Nephi 28:31, Ether 12:38); what is particular here is the pairing with 'set at nought', which no other Book of Mormon occurrence has.

pericopes.text: For behold that all little children are alive in Christ, and also all they that are without the law. For the power of redemption cometh on all they that have no law; wherefore, he that is not condemned, or he that is under no condemnation, cannot repent; and unto such baptism availeth nothing.

links.text: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.

provenance.route: Romans 8:1, with Romans 5:13 and 4:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “no condemnation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:1, 'There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus'. “sin is not imputed when there is no law” is a KJV singleton at Romans 5:13, and Romans 4:15's 'where no law is, there is no transgression' states the same rule.
provenance.significance: Moroni 8:22 is Romans compressed. Romans 8:1 gives 'no condemnation' and 'in Christ'; Romans 5:13 and 4:15 give the rule that where there is no law there is no imputed sin; Romans 2:12 gives 'as many as have sinned without law'. Put together, they yield exactly the chapter's conclusion — that those under no law are under no condemnation, and that repentance, being the remedy for condemnation, has no object in them. The interest is that Paul's 'no condemnation' is a status won by being in Christ, and Moroni 8:22 extends it to those who never left, so that the phrase describes an innocence rather than an acquittal.

links.note: “For behold that all little children are alive in Christ, and also all they that are without the law… he that is not condemned, or he that is under no condemnation, cannot repent.” One verse carrying three of Romans's rare formulations: 'in Christ' with 'no condemnation' from 8:1, 'without the law' and 'have no law' from 2:12 and 5:13, and behind them Romans 4:15's principle. This is the Romans contact the chapter has been building toward since 8:8's curse of Adam, and it is where the argument is actually made rather than asserted. Note the syllogism's second premise is supplied by 8:24 ('repentance is unto them that are under condemnation'), which is Mormon's own, not Paul's.

pericopes.text: But it is mockery before God, denying the mercies of Christ, and the power of his holy spirit, and putting trust in dead works.

links.text: Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,

provenance.other: “dead works” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hebrews 6:1 ('repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God') and Hebrews 9:14 ('purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God'). Moroni 8:23 reads 'putting trust in dead works'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 6:1-2 lists the foundational doctrines in a fixed order: repentance from dead works, faith toward God, the doctrine of baptisms, laying on of hands. Moroni 8:23-26 runs the same list, in the same order, as a chain of causes — dead works rejected (8:23), repentance and baptism (8:25), baptism by faith unto remission (8:25), and then the visitation of the Holy Ghost (8:26), which in Hebrews' list is what the laying on of hands is for. The catechism Hebrews calls the principles Moroni 8 turns into a sequence, and the point of the sequence is that nothing in it can be entered at the wrong end.

links.note: “And putting trust in dead works.” Two KJV verses have 'dead works' and both are in Hebrews; the one that also has repentance and baptism in the next breath is Hebrews 6:1-2, and it is that list, not the phrase alone, that the following three verses of Moroni 8 reproduce. Mormon's change is the verb: Hebrews speaks of repentance *from* dead works, Moroni of putting *trust in* them, which is the sharper charge and is aimed at a rite rather than at a life. Hebrews 9:14's 'purge your conscience' stands behind 8:26's chain from remission to the visitation of the Spirit.

pericopes.text: Behold, my son, this thing had not ought to be: for repentance is unto them that are under condemnation, and under the curse of a broken law.

links.text: For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them.

provenance.other: “under the curse” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 3:10, 'as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse'. Galatians 3:13 supplies the release, 'Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law'.
provenance.significance: Galatians is the letter that argues a rite of initiation cannot be required of those the promise already covers, which is Moroni 8's thesis with circumcision in the place of baptism — and 8:8 has already invoked circumcision by name. Under Galatians 3:10 those under the curse are those who rely on the works of the law; under Moroni 8:24 they are those for whom repentance is meant. The borrowed phrase therefore carries a hidden compliment to the chapter's opponents' opposite: those who cannot break a law cannot be cursed by it.

links.note: “For repentance is unto them that are under condemnation, and under the curse of a broken law.” The KJV's one 'under the curse' verse, with 'of a broken law' supplying what Galatians 3:10 states in its next clause. Moderate rather than high because 'under the curse' is a natural English phrase and the sentence is also continuous with 8:22's Romans material; the reason for preferring Galatians is that the chapter has already used Galatians 6:7 at 8:9 and is arguing the Galatians case about circumcision at 8:8. The 1830's word order here — 'this thing had not ought to be' — was rearranged in 1920 to 'ought not', a grammatical correction with no bearing on the source.

pericopes.text: And the first fruits of repentance is baptism; and baptism cometh by faith, unto the fulfilling the commandments; and the fulfilling the commandments bringeth remission of sins;

and the remission of sins bringeth meekness, and lowliness of heart; and because of meekness and lowliness of heart, cometh the visitation of the Holy Ghost, which comforter filleth with hope and perfect love, which love endureth by diligence unto prayer, until the end shall come, when all the saints shall dwell with God.

links.text: Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “fill you with all joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “abound in hope” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both being Romans 15:13, which also ends 'through the power of the Holy Ghost'. “the Comforter” as a title of the Spirit occurs in three KJV verses, all in John.
provenance.significance: Romans 15:13 is the KJV's one verse joining a filling, hope, and the Holy Ghost in a single sentence, and Moroni 8:26 joins the same three — 'the visitation of the Holy Ghost, which comforter filleth with hope'. What Moroni adds is John's title for the Spirit, so that Paul's benediction is spoken about the Johannine Comforter; and what it adds after that is 'and perfect love', which brings 1 John 4:18 back from 8:16 to close the chain.

links.note: “Cometh the visitation of the Holy Ghost, which comforter filleth with hope and perfect love.” Two KJV singletons stand in Romans 15:13 and the verse's own subject is a filling with hope by the Holy Ghost, which is Moroni's clause with the terms in the same relation. The row is moderate because no run of words is shared: the contact is the unusual predication ('filleth with hope') plus the agent, not the phrasing. 'Comforter' is John's word, not Paul's, so the sentence is a composite; and the chain it closes — remission, meekness, visitation, hope, love, endurance to the end — is the same catechetical order as Hebrews 6:1-2 at 8:23.
links.whyNot: No verbal run is shared with Romans 15:13; a reader may take 'filleth with hope' as ordinary devotional English and read the verse as wholly Mormon's own.

pericopes.text: Behold, my son, I will write unto you again, if I go not out soon against the Lamanites. Behold, the pride of this nation, or the people of the Nephites, hath proved their destruction, except they should repent.

Pray for them, my son, that repentance may come unto them. But behold, I fear lest the spirit hath ceased striving with them; and in this part of the land they are also seeking to put down all power and authority, which cometh from God; and they are denying the Holy Ghost.

links.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.other: “strive with man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:3, 'My spirit shall not always strive with man'. The Book of Mormon uses the clause six times and every occurrence stands at a threatened or completed destruction.
provenance.significance: Genesis 6:3 is the sentence immediately preceding the Flood — the withdrawal of the Spirit is the notice that a people is about to be destroyed, and the hundred and twenty years is the term of grace. Mormon writes it of the Nephites four verses before the end of his letter, having already told Moroni at 8:27 that pride 'hath proved their destruction'. He had used the same clause at Mormon 5:16 of the same people; here it is put in the mildest available form ('I fear lest') and addressed to his son, which makes it a private admission of what the record will report publicly.

links.note: “But behold, I fear lest the spirit hath ceased striving with them.” The KJV's one 'strive with man' verse, and the Book of Mormon's standing formula for a nation past saving. The link is written here rather than cross-referenced because this is a different book and a different voice from the earlier adjudications — Mormon in a private letter rather than a narrator in a chronicle — and because the verb has changed aspect: Genesis and the earlier occurrences say the Spirit shall not always strive, Moroni 8:28 fears it has already ceased, which is the same sentence after the term of grace has run out.

links.text: Then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father; when he shall have put down all rule and all authority and power.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 15:24 with Romans 13:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “put down all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “all rule and all authority” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both being 1 Corinthians 15:24, 'when he shall have put down all rule and all authority and power'. “no power but of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 13:1, 'the powers that be are ordained of God'.
provenance.significance: The reversal is the interest. In 1 Corinthians 15:24 it is Christ who puts down all rule and authority and power, at the end, as the last act of his reign; in Moroni 8:28 it is the apostate Nephites who are 'seeking to put down all power and authority', and the reason it is wickedness rather than eschatology is the clause Mormon attaches from Romans 13:1 — 'which cometh from God'. The same act belongs to Christ and damns anyone else.

links.note: “They are also seeking to put down all power and authority, which cometh from God.” Two KJV singletons in one clause, both from 1 Corinthians 15:24, with Romans 13:1's doctrine of ordained power supplying the relative clause. 1 Corinthians 15 is already in the chapter at 8:12 (verse 22), which raises the prior odds that verse 24 is being reached for here. Moderate rather than high because the shared wording is a common enough political idiom and because the sense is inverted; the case rests on the two singletons falling in the same source verse.
links.whyNot: 'Put down all power and authority' is ordinary English for suppressing government, and the source verse means the opposite of what Moroni 8:28 means by it. A reader may reasonably treat the coincidence as accidental.

pericopes.text: And after rejecting so great a knowledge, my son, they must perish soon, unto the fulfilling of the prophecies which was spoken by the prophets, as well as the words of our Saviour himself.

links.text: How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him;

provenance.other: “so great salvation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 2:3, 'How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him'. “so great a” is common (six verses) and identifies nothing on its own.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 2:3 grounds the inescapability of the judgment in the chain of transmission — spoken by the Lord, confirmed by those who heard him. Moroni 8:29 grounds the destruction in the same chain and names both links: 'the prophecies which was spoken by the prophets, as well as the words of our Saviour himself'. Hebrews asks a question; Moroni answers it about a particular people.

links.note: “And after rejecting so great a knowledge, my son, they must perish soon.” The KJV forms 'so great' with an abstract noun of salvation once, and its argument — no escape for those who neglect what was spoken by the Lord and confirmed by his hearers — is the argument of the whole verse here, down to Moroni's pairing of the prophets with 'the words of our Saviour himself'. Recorded as an echo because the shared element is a two-word phrase with the noun changed, from salvation to knowledge; the case is the argument the phrase brings with it, not the phrase. 1830 reads 'which was spoken', corrected to 'were' in 1920, and 'Saviour', modernized to 'Savior'.
links.whyNot: 'So great a knowledge' shares only 'so great' with Hebrews 2:3, and 'so great a' occurs in six KJV verses; a reader who requires the noun to match should decline this row.

pericopes.text: Farewell, my son, until I shall write unto you, or shall meet you again. Amen.

links.text: Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full.

provenance.route: 2 John 1:12 and 3 John 1:13-14 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “many things to write unto you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 John 1:12; 3 John 1:13-14 says the same thing in the singular and adds 'I trust I shall shortly see thee'. “farewell” occurs in four KJV verses, of which 2 Corinthians 13:11 is the only letter-closing.
provenance.significance: The Johannine letters close on a disjunction — more to write, or a meeting face to face, and the writer prefers the meeting. Moroni 8:27 and 8:30 hold the same disjunction and reverse its confidence: 'if I go not out soon against the Lamanites', 'until I shall write unto you, or shall meet you again'. In the epistles the alternative to writing is a visit the writer expects; in Moroni 8 both branches are in doubt because the writer expects to be killed, and the reader of the Book of Mormon already knows he was.

links.note: “Farewell, my son, until I shall write unto you, or shall meet you again. Amen.” The chapter closes in the form its opening announced (see 8:2, 2 Timothy 1:2): a letter, and specifically a New Testament letter, with a farewell and the write-or-see-you disjunction that ends 2 and 3 John. The verbal contact is slight — 'write unto you' and 'farewell' — and the row is offered for the form rather than the phrasing, which is why it is an echo. Note that 8:27's 'I will write unto you again, if I go not out soon against the Lamanites' is the same construction with the reason for doubt supplied, and that Mormon does write again: Moroni 9.
links.whyNot: 'Farewell' and 'write unto you' are the common property of every letter in English, and the epistolary form of Moroni 8 could be borrowed at the level of genre without any particular verse behind this one.

pericopes.text: My beloved son, I write unto you again, that ye may know that I am yet alive; but I write somewhat that which is grievous.

links.text: For I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck: behold, while I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the LORD; and how much more after my death?

provenance.other: “I am yet alive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 31:27. The near neighbours are all interrogative or third-person — 'Is your father yet alive?' (Genesis 43:27), 'while the child was yet alive' (2 Samuel 12:21) — and none of them is a man saying it of himself.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the KJV's one first-person 'I am yet alive' is Moses, at the end of his life, handing over a written record and telling Israel that they rebel while he is with them and will be worse when he is gone: 'I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves' (31:29). Moroni 9 is that verse's contents. Mormon writes 'that ye may know that I am yet alive', hands the sacred records to his son (9:24), forecasts the people's 'utter destruction' (9:22), and the twenty-four verses in between are the corruption Moses predicted for after his own death. The borrowing, if it is one, puts Mormon in Moses' chair at exactly the moment the succession is being made.

links.note: 'I write unto you again, that ye may know that I am yet alive.' The phrase is a KJV singleton and its one occurrence is the Deuteronomic farewell — a dying leader's last written charge, whose subject is the people's corruption after his death. Mormon's letter is that same document: written, valedictory, and about the corruption. The verbal contact is four words and the phrase is natural English for a letter reporting survival, which is why this sits at moderate rather than higher; the contextual fit is what carries it. Compare Hays on metalepsis — the words are ordinary, the recovered setting is not.
links.whyNot: 'I am yet alive' is the plainest possible way to say the thing Mormon is saying, and a writer with no verse in mind would arrive at it. Nothing else of Deuteronomy 31 is verbally present.

pericopes.text: For behold, I have had a sore battle with the Lamanites, in the which we did not conquer; and Archeantus has fallen by the sword, and also Luram and Emron; yea, and we have lost a great number of our choice men.
And now behold, my son, I fear lest the Lamanites shall destroy this people, for they do not repent, and Satan stirreth them up continually to anger, one with another.

Behold, I am laboring with them continually; and when I speak the word of God with sharpness, they tremble and anger against me; and when I use no sharpness, they harden their hearts against it; wherefore I fear lest the spirit of the Lord hath ceased striving with them.

links.text: Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction.

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 13:10 + Acts 4:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon (the same fusion already made at Words of Mormon 1:17)
provenance.other: “Sharpness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 13:10, and “use sharpness” in that same one. The frame “the word of God with —” is also a KJV singleton, Acts 4:31's 'they spake the word of God with boldness'. Moroni 9:4 has both at once: 'I speak the word of God with sharpness'.
provenance.significance: The one KJV verse that uses this word is a letter-writer explaining why he is severe on paper: Paul writes 'being absent' precisely so that he need not 'use sharpness' when present, and grounds the severity in a power given 'to edification, and not to destruction'. Mormon is in Paul's exact position — absent, writing, and weighing how hard to press — but the calculus has failed at both settings: sharpness makes them tremble and rage, no sharpness lets them harden. Paul's alternative between edification and destruction has collapsed into destruction only, which is the sentence Mormon reaches in the same verse: 'the spirit of the Lord hath ceased striving with them.'

links.note: The chapter's single strongest verbal row and one the n-gram stream ranked below a Job verse. Two KJV singletons meet in one clause — Acts 4:31's frame for speaking the word of God 'with' something, and 2 Corinthians 13:10's 'sharpness' — and the same pair was already fused at Words of Mormon 1:17 ('they did speak the word of God, with power and with authority; and they did use much sharpness'). Moroni 9:4 is a different book and a different hand's letter, so the row is written here rather than deferred (ADJUDICATING §4); the argument for the fusion was made at Words of Mormon and is not restated. What is new here is that Moroni 9:4 supplies the negative half Paul's verse implies and never states — 'when I use no sharpness' — and reports that it fails too.

links.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.other: “Strive with man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:3. The Book of Mormon's own form is fixed at 2 Nephi 26:11 — 'the Spirit of the Lord will not always strive with man' — and Moroni 9:4's proximate model is Mormon 5:16, 'the Spirit of the Lord hath already ceased to strive with them', which is the same writer saying the same thing about the same people one book earlier.
provenance.significance: Genesis 6:3 is the sentence God speaks immediately before the Flood, and the clause that follows it is the verdict that 'the wickedness of man was great in the earth'. The Book of Mormon has kept the phrase as a threshold marker — 2 Nephi 26:11 states it as a law, Ether 2:15 applies it to the Jaredites, Ether 15:19 records it spent. By Moroni 9:4 Mormon reports it crossed for his own people, and at 9:23 he names the Jaredites as the precedent. The Genesis verse is therefore doing structural work: the corpus's two civilisations end at the same sentence, and Mormon knows it.

links.note: 'Wherefore I fear lest the spirit of the Lord hath ceased striving with them.' The KJV singleton is Genesis 6:3 and the tense is the finding: Genesis states a limit, and Moroni 9:4 reports it reached. The proximate model is not the Bible but Mormon 5:16, where the same author wrote 'hath already ceased to strive with them' of the same nation — hence mediation 'OT-via-earlier-BoM'. 1830 reads 'ceased striving', a participial form found in neither the KJV nor Mormon 5:16, so the phrase has been re-cast rather than copied.

pericopes.text: For so exceedingly do they anger, that it seemeth me that they have no fear of death; and they have lost their love, one towards another; and they thirst after blood and revenge continually.

links.text: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.

provenance.route: Matthew 5:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the Beatitude is already in the corpus at 3 Nephi 12:6
provenance.other: “Thirst after” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:6, where its object is righteousness. “Love of many shall wax cold” is a KJV singleton at Matthew 24:12, and “love one toward another” occurs in five verses of which 1 Thessalonians 3:12 is the prayer that it increase. “Blood and revenge” occurs nowhere in the KJV and nowhere else in the Book of Mormon: only here and at 9:23.
provenance.significance: The one thing the KJV thirsts after is righteousness, and Moroni 9:5 substitutes blood and revenge — then 9:6, the next verse, names 'the enemy of all righteousness' as what is to be conquered. Righteousness is demonstrably the word in play across the two verses, which is why the substitution reads as one rather than as coincidence. The Beatitude promises the thirsty 'they shall be filled'; the flesh of 9:8 is the filling this people receives.

links.note: 'They have lost their love, one towards another; and they thirst after blood and revenge continually.' Two moves in one clause, both of them inversions of KJV formulas: love 'one toward another' is what 1 Thessalonians 3:12 prays God will increase and what Matthew 24:12 says will wax cold when iniquity abounds, and 'thirst after' is the Beatitude's verb with its object exchanged. Neither half is verbally heavy, and Matthew 24:12 supplies only the idea. The row rests on the singleton verb plus the fact that 9:6 immediately produces 'righteousness' as the missing object.
links.whyNot: 'Thirst after' is two ordinary words and 'blood and revenge' is the writer's own coinage, used again nineteen verses later. A reader who thinks Mormon simply wrote plain English about bloodthirst is not refuted by anything here except the neighbouring 'righteousness'.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved son, notwithstanding their hardness, let us labor diligently: for if we should cease to labor, we should be brought under condemnation: for we have a labor to perform whilst in this tabernacle of clay, that we may conquer the enemy of all righteousness, and rest our souls in the kingdom of God.

links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.route: Acts 13:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon. The proximate model is very likely the corpus's own established title for the devil (Mosiah 4:14, Alma 30:22 and the rest) rather than Acts directly — but the schema's 'OT-via-earlier-BoM' has no NT counterpart, so this is recorded as 'direct-NT' with the route stated here. FLAGGED as a conventions gap.
provenance.other: “Enemy of all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10. Esther 9:24's 'the enemy of all the Jews' is the only other KJV 'enemy of all —' and is a different construction with a different referent; it is filed in the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: In Acts the title is thrown at a man — Elymas the sorcerer, blinded on the spot for withstanding the word — and the charge is that he will not 'cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord'. The Book of Mormon has made the same words a name for the devil, and Moroni 9:6 sets them against a labour that must not cease: 'if we should cease to labor, we should be brought under condemnation.' The verb Acts uses of the enemy's refusal to cease is the verb Mormon refuses to let himself perform.

links.note: A KJV singleton, reproduced whole. The phrase is by this point the corpus's standing title for the devil, adjudicated first at 1 Nephi 13:27, and Moroni is a new book with a new voice, so the row is written here rather than deferred (ADJUDICATING §4) and the argument for the borrowing itself is at 1 Nephi 13:27. What Moroni 9:6 adds is the pairing with 'cease': Acts 13:10 asks the enemy of all righteousness whether he will not cease, and Mormon answers for himself that he will not.

links.text: How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed before the moth?

provenance.other: “Tabernacle of clay” occurs in no KJV verse. Its two halves each have a source: “houses of clay” is a KJV singleton at Job 4:19, and the body-as-tabernacle is 2 Corinthians 5:1 ('our earthly house of this tabernacle') and 2 Peter 1:13-14. The compound is the Book of Mormon's own, minted at Mosiah 3:5.
provenance.significance: Job 4:19 is Eliphaz arguing that a creature housed in clay cannot be trusted to be righteous before God; Moroni 9:6 uses the same housing to argue the opposite — that the clay is exactly where the labour has to be done, 'whilst in this tabernacle of clay'. The verse turns a reason for futility into a deadline.

links.note: The compound is not a KJV phrase and is not claimed as one. It is the corpus's own fusion of a Job singleton with the Pauline tabernacle, coined at Mosiah 3:5 in the angel's speech to Benjamin, and Moroni 9:6 is a different book reusing it. Recorded at moderate because the dependence is on the Book of Mormon's compound rather than on either biblical verse directly; mediation is left 'uncertain' because neither half's wording is decisive about which route reached the compound.

pericopes.text: And now I write somewhat concerning the sufferings of this people. For according to the knowledge which I have received from Amoron, behold, the Lamanites have many prisoners, which they took from the tower of Sherrizah; and there were men, women and children.

And the husbands and fathers of those women and children they have slain; and they feed the women upon the flesh of their husbands, and the children upon the flesh of their fathers; and no water, save a little, do they give unto them.

links.text: Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds.

provenance.route: the KJV covenant-curse cannibalism topos (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57; Jeremiah 19:9; Lamentations 4:10; Ezekiel 4:16-5:10) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The sons shall eat their fathers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 5:10, and it is the only place in the Bible where the eating runs UP the generations rather than down. “The flesh of their —” occurs in two verses, of which Jeremiah 19:9 is the siege one; “the flesh of his friend” is a Jeremiah 19:9 singleton. “The pitiful women have sodden their own children” is a Lamentations 4:10 singleton. Every other member of the cluster — Leviticus 26:29, Deuteronomy 28:53-57 — has parents eating children.
provenance.significance: The topos exists in scripture for one purpose: it is the last curse in the covenant list, the sign that the sanctions have run out. Deuteronomy 28 puts it 'in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee', and Ezekiel pairs it with the water ration ('they shall drink water by measure', 4:16) that Moroni 9:8 also has: 'no water, save a little, do they give unto them.' Two members of one Ezekiel oracle, four verses apart, appear in one Book of Mormon sentence. What the sentence then does with them is the finding — see the note.

links.note: The biblical cannibalism of siege is a famine act by the starving: parents eat their own children because there is nothing else, and the horror is that hunger has undone kinship. Moroni 9:8 inverts every term. The eating is not done by the hungry but imposed by captors; the victims are fed, not driven; and the flesh is a husband's and a father's, which runs up the generations, not down. Ezekiel 5:10 is the one KJV verse that runs that direction, which is why it is named as the source rather than the more famous Deuteronomy 28:53. The dependence on the topos is not seriously deniable — the water ration in the same sentence settles it — but the choice among its members is a judgment, and this verse is deliberately worse than any of them: where scripture's curse is what famine does to a people, Moroni 9:8 is what a people does to a people with food still in hand.
links.whyNot: No single KJV verse is verbally decisive here; Moroni 9:8 shares no run of four words with any member of the cluster. A reader could hold that the passage draws on the general biblical vocabulary of atrocity rather than on Ezekiel 5:10 in particular, and the evidence would not refute him — the case for Ezekiel specifically rests on the direction of the eating and on the water ration four verses earlier.

pericopes.text: And notwithstanding this great abomination of the Lamanites, it doth not exceed that of our people in Moriantum. For behold, many of the daughters of the Lamanites have they taken prisoners; and after depriving them of that which was most dear and precious above all things, which is chastity and virtue;

and after that they had done this thing, they did murder them in a most cruel manner, torturing their bodies even unto death; and after that they have done this, they devour their flesh like unto wild beasts, because of the hardness of their hearts; and they do it for a token of bravery.

links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “Hardness of their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5. Matthew 19:8's 'hardness of your hearts' is the second-person form and is a different verse; the machine proposed it here and it is filed in the exclusion register. The Book of Mormon uses each form in its correct grammatical setting, and Moroni 9:10, being narration about a third party, takes Mark's.
provenance.significance: Mark 3:5 is the one verse in the Gospels where Jesus is angry, and the anger is grief — 'when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts' — and it issues in a hand restored. Moroni 9:10 borrows the diagnosis and reverses the outcome: the hardness here issues in bodies torn rather than a body healed, and the letter that contains it is written by a man whose anger is entirely grief. Mormon is looking round about on them with anger for the same reason and can restore nothing.

links.note: The corpus's standing phrase for the condition it diagnoses, adjudicated first at 1 Nephi 2:18 and used nine further times before this. Moroni is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4), so the row is written rather than deferred, and the argument for the borrowing is at 1 Nephi 2:18. Two things are worth adding here. First the pronoun, which is the trap: 'their', not Matthew 19:8's 'your', and correctly so for third-person narration. Second the placement — in every earlier occurrence the hardness explains a refusal to hear; here for the first time it explains cannibalism, and the same six words are asked to carry it.

pericopes.text: O my beloved son, how can a people like this, that are without civilization;
(and only a few years have passed away, and they were a civil and a delightsome people;)

links.text: And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts.

provenance.route: Malachi 3:12 → KJV → 2 Nephi 5:21 and the corpus's own 'delightsome' formula → Moroni 9:12. Malachi 3 is transcribed wholesale at 3 Nephi 24, so the source verse is inside the Book of Mormon as well as behind it.
provenance.other: “Delightsome” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Malachi 3:12, where it qualifies a LAND. Every Book of Mormon use but this one qualifies a PEOPLE.
provenance.significance: Malachi 3:12 is a promise conditional on the tithe: bring the offerings and 'all nations shall call you blessed'. The Book of Mormon transcribes that promise at 3 Nephi 24:12 and then, sixty years of narrative later, Mormon reaches for its one distinctive word to say that the condition has been withdrawn — 'only a few years have passed away, and they were a civil and a delightsome people'. The tense is the whole argument. Malachi's word appears in this chapter only in the past.

links.note: The word is a KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon's use of it is by this point its own idiom, fixed at 2 Nephi 5:21 and running through 4 Nephi 1:10's account of the golden age this chapter is the ruin of. Moroni 9:12 is the corpus's last 'delightsome', and it is in the past tense inside a parenthesis. Recorded at moderate: one word, however rare, is thin evidence for direct dependence on Malachi, and the mediation call — through the corpus's own formula rather than the KJV verse — is where the confidence actually sits.

pericopes.text: but O my son, how can a people like this, whose delight is in so much abomination,
how can we expect that God will stay his hand in judgement against us?

links.text: And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?

provenance.other: “Stay his hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 4:35, and it is of God's hand. The 1830 text reads 'judgement'; 1920 modernized to 'judgment'.
provenance.significance: Daniel 4 is the chapter in which a man is driven from among men, eats grass as oxen, and grows hair like eagles' feathers and nails like birds' claws — the one biblical narrative of a human being reduced to a beast — and 4:35 is the sentence he speaks when his reason returns. Four verses before Moroni 9:14, Mormon has written that his people 'devour their flesh like unto wild beasts'. The KJV's only 'stay his hand' therefore comes out of the one chapter where the alternative to God's judgment is not death but bestiality, which is precisely the condition Moroni 9:9-10 has just described. Nebuchadnezzar's beast-years ended when he looked up; Mormon asks his question because he does not expect his people to.

links.note: 'How can we expect that God will stay his hand in judgement against us?' A KJV singleton with its verb and object intact, and the grammar turned around as it was at Alma 10:23 — in Daniel nobody CAN stay God's hand, in Moroni nobody should EXPECT him to. Alma 10:23 is where that inversion was adjudicated; the argument is not restated. What Moroni 9:14 adds is the neighbourhood: Daniel 4's king becomes a beast and Moroni 9:10's people devour flesh like wild beasts, and the shared phrase sits between the two. Moderate rather than high because three words is a small purchase and the inversion means the sense is not reproduced, only the collocation.

pericopes.text: Behold, my heart cries wo unto this people. Come out in judgement, O God, and hide their sins, and wickedness, and abominations from before thy face.

links.text: Hide thy face from my sins, and blot out all mine iniquities.

provenance.other: “Hide thy face from my sins” is a KJV singleton at Psalm 51:9. The exact string Moroni 9:15 uses, “from before thy face”, is also a KJV singleton — Deuteronomy 28:31, of an ass violently taken away — but the sense there is unrelated and it is filed in the exclusion register. The 1830 text reads 'judgement'; 1920 modernized to 'judgment'.
provenance.significance: Psalm 51 is the penitent's prayer, and its request is that God look away from sins the psalmist owns. Moroni 9:15 makes the same request on behalf of a people who are not repenting and in the same breath asks God to 'come out in judgement' — the two halves of the sentence pull against each other, and the Psalm is where the softer half comes from. If the echo is real, Mormon is praying David's prayer for men who have not asked for it.

links.note: 'Come out in judgement, O God, and hide their sins, and wickedness, and abominations from before thy face.' The clause is odd on its face — judgment and concealment asked for at once — and the KJV's one prayer that God hide his face from sins is Psalm 51:9. The verbal contact is 'hide', 'face', 'sins', with the possessive moved from the sinner to God, which is not much. Recorded because the oddity of the sentence is real and the Psalm makes it read as intercession rather than confusion.
links.whyNot: Three ordinary words in a different arrangement, and the direction is reversed: David asks God to hide his own face from sins, Mormon asks God to hide the sins from his face. A reader may fairly say this is Mormon's own phrasing of an intercession and that no verse stands behind it. The machine's proposal at this verse, Deuteronomy 28:31, matches the string exactly and is worse.

pericopes.text: And again, my son, there are many widows and their daughters, which remain in Sherrizah; and that part of the provisions which the Lamanites did not carry away, behold, the army of Zenephi has carried away, and left them to wander withersoever they can for food; and many old women do faint by the way and die.

links.text: And if I send them away fasting to their own houses, they will faint by the way: for divers of them came from far.

provenance.other: “Faint by the way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 8:3. Matthew's parallel at 15:32 reads 'lest they faint in the way', with the other preposition — so the Book of Mormon has Mark's form, not Matthew's, and the distinction is a single word.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one 'faint by the way' is Jesus refusing to let it happen. Mark 8:1-9 is the feeding of the four thousand, and 8:3 is the reason given for the miracle: he will not send a hungry crowd home because they will faint on the road. Moroni 9:16 is that verse with the miracle withheld. The provisions exist — the Lamanites took part and the army of Zenephi carried away the rest — and the women are sent out to 'wander withersoever they can for food', and they faint by the way and die. Recover Mark's context and the sentence acquires the thing it does not say: this is what happens where nobody multiplies the loaves.

links.note: A KJV singleton reproduced exactly, in a verse about hunger, and the preposition is Mark's rather than Matthew's — 'by the way', not 'in the way'. The machine stream did not propose it; contiguous windows found only 'and the army which' two verses on. This is the chapter's clearest metalepsis (compare Hays): the one biblical use of the phrase is a refusal to send the hungry away, and Moroni 9:16's old women have been sent away by both armies at once.

pericopes.text: And the army which is with me, is weak; and the armies of the Lamanites are betwixt Sherrizah and me; and as many as have fled to the army of Aaron, have fallen victims to their awful brutality.
O the depravity of my people! they are without order and without mercy. Behold, I am but a man, and I have but the strength of a man, and I cannot any longer enforce my commands;
